items.title: Formation du gouvernement : Le PPS choisit de rejoindre la majorité
items.description: Le Parti du progrès et du socialisme (PPS) a tranché. Réuni lundi 12 octobre au matin à son siège national, à Rabat, le bureau politique de la formation a opté pour la participation au prochain gouvernement, au terme de délibérations internes et de consultations avec la cheffe du gouvernement, Fatima Zahra El Mansouri, chargée de former le nouvel exécutif. Cette décision intervient à la suite de la réunion du comité central du parti et des discussions engagées avec la cheffe du gouvernement désignée. Dans un communiqué publié à l’issue de sa réunion, le PPS présente ce choix comme le plus approprié au regard du contexte politique actuel et de sa volonté de contribuer à la poursuite des réformes dans le pays. Pour arrêter sa position, le bureau politique indique avoir tenu compte des débats « approfondis et responsables » qui ont marqué la réunion du comité central, ainsi que des échanges menés en son sein. Il a également pris en considération les orientations envisagées pour le prochain programme gouvernemental et celles d’une future charte de la majorité, dont la formation est en cours de négociation. La configuration politique et partisane de la majorité appelée à soutenir le nouvel exécutif a également pesé dans la réflexion. Le PPS souligne, en outre, le climat positif des négociations avec la cheffe du gouvernement désignée, caractérisé, selon le parti, par la confiance et une forte convergence sur les orientations fondamentales et les points de vue. Une participation placée sous le signe des réformes S’appuyant sur le mandat confié par le comité central, le bureau politique estime que la participation au gouvernement constitue, dans les circonstances actuelles, la meilleure option pour permettre au PPS de prendre part activement à la dynamique de réforme du pays. Le parti entend notamment contribuer à la consolidation du processus démocratique, à la préservation des libertés et des droits, à la moralisation de la vie publique et au renforcement de la justice sociale et territoriale. Le développement des capacités de l’économie nationale figure également parmi les objectifs avancés pour justifier ce choix. Cette orientation traduit la volonté du PPS de prendre part à l’action gouvernementale tout en mettant en avant ses priorités politiques et sociales. Le communiqué ne précise toutefois ni les portefeuilles ministériels susceptibles de lui revenir ni les modalités concrètes de sa participation au futur exécutif. Le parti affirme vouloir faire de cette présence au gouvernement une contribution « effective et efficace, audacieuse et responsable ». Il entend ainsi apporter une « véritable valeur ajoutée » aux réformes et à la consolidation des acquis, en s’engageant à agir dans le respect de l’intérêt général. Le PPS insiste enfin sur la nécessité de fonder cette participation sur l’engagement, la fidélité aux engagements pris et le respect profond et constant des exigences du service de l’intérêt général. La composition politique du prochain gouvernement doit encore être annoncée, alors que les consultations destinées à former la nouvelle majorité se poursuivent. items.title: Al Salam Bank Algérie accélère sa digitalisation
items.description: Al Salam Bank Algérie a participé à la 5ᵉ édition d’ ECSEL Expo , le salon dédié au commerce électronique et aux services en ligne, organisé du 7 au 10 octobre 2026 au Palais des Expositions – SAFEX, à Alger. Avec plus de 260 exposants annoncés, cette édition a réuni des entreprises, des professionnels et des acteurs de l’écosystème numérique autour des évolutions du commerce électronique en Algérie. Le développement des usages numériques fait évoluer les besoins des particuliers, des commerçants et des entreprises en matière de paiement, d’accès aux services bancaires à distance et de gestion des opérations financières. Dans ce contexte, la participation d’Al Salam Bank Algérie à ECSEL Expo s’inscrit dans une démarche d’échange avec les acteurs de l’économie numérique et d’identification des besoins auxquels les services bancaires peuvent répondre. Comment les banques peuvent-elles accompagner l’évolution des usages numériques en Algérie ? Quelles solutions Al Salam Bank met-elle à la disposition de ses clients et quelles perspectives de collaboration offre le développement du commerce électronique ? Source: DR Azouz Abdelmalek, responsable de la cellule marketing et communication au sein d’Al Salam Bank Algérie, répond à nos questions dans cet entretien accordé à TSA. Source : DR Pourquoi la digitalisation est-elle devenue incontournable dans le secteur bancaire en Algérie ? Azouz Abdelmalek : La digitalisation accompagne l’évolution des usages et des attentes des clients. Avec le développement du commerce électronique et des paiements en ligne, les particuliers comme les entreprises recherchent des moyens plus pratiques d’accéder aux services bancaires et d’effectuer leurs opérations à distance. Cette évolution s’inscrit dans la dynamique de développement des paiements électroniques et d’inclusion financière portée par les acteurs du secteur bancaire en Algérie. Chez Al Salam Bank Algérie, nous avons fait du digital un axe de développement de notre offre de services. Cette orientation se traduit notamment par le développement d’applications bancaires permettant aux clients d’effectuer certaines opérations à distance, ainsi que par des solutions destinées aux professionnels et aux entreprises. L’enjeu est de proposer des services adaptés aux nouveaux usages, tout en maintenant un accompagnement qui tient compte des besoins de chaque catégorie de clientèle. De nouveaux besoins en matière de paiement, de gestion des opérations financières et d’accès aux services bancaires sont apparus, notamment chez les commerçants, les entreprises et les professionnels. Comment Al Salam Bank répond-elle à ces attentes ? Azouz Abdelmalek : Les besoins diffèrent selon les profils. Pour les particuliers, l’accès à distance aux opérations courantes représente une possibilité de simplifier certaines démarches. Pour les commerçants et les entreprises, les enjeux concernent notamment l’exécution des virements, le suivi des mouvements financiers, les encaissements et la gestion de la trésorerie. Notre approche consiste à développer des services numériques correspondant à ces différents besoins. Elle repose également sur l’évolution de nos pratiques internes et sur l'accompagnement de nos collaborateurs dans l'utilisation des outils digitaux. Nous accordons notamment une attention particulière aux plateformes d'échange et de formation intégrant l'intelligence artificielle, afin de soutenir le développement des compétences numériques de nos équipes. Cette démarche s'accompagne d'initiatives visant à réduire l'utilisation du papier grâce aux plateformes numériques de la banque et à faciliter le suivi à distance des opérations des clients. Pour autant, le digital ne se substitue pas à la relation humaine. Il constitue un moyen supplémentaire de faciliter les démarches et d'adapter les services bancaires aux attentes des clients, dans le respect des principes de la finance islamique. Quelle approche privilégiez-vous pour accompagner la transformation numérique des services bancaires ? Azouz Abdelmalek : Nous privilégions une approche qui part des usages et des besoins de nos clients. La transformation numérique ne consiste pas uniquement à transposer des opérations sur une application : elle implique aussi de réfléchir aux démarches que les clients peuvent effectuer à distance et aux services dont ils ont besoin pour gérer leurs opérations. Cette approche se traduit par le développement de solutions destinées aux particuliers, notamment à travers MySalam+ , et aux professionnels et aux entreprises, avec MySalam Pro . Elle concerne également nos méthodes de travail et l'accompagnement de nos collaborateurs dans l'appropriation des outils numériques. Nous travaillons ainsi sur plusieurs dimensions complémentaires : l'accès aux services bancaires à distance, l'évolution des parcours clients et l'utilisation des outils digitaux en interne. Notre objectif est de faire évoluer progressivement notre offre en fonction des besoins identifiés, tout en préservant la possibilité d'un accompagnement personnalisé lorsque la situation du client le nécessite. Quels services bancaires Al Salam Bank met-elle à la disposition de ses clients particuliers, professionnels et entreprises à l'heure de la numérisation ? Azouz Abdelmalek : Nous proposons plusieurs services numériques destinés à faciliter l'accès aux opérations bancaires. Pour les particuliers, l'application MySalam+ permet notamment de consulter les comptes et les opérations, d'effectuer des virements et d'accéder à différents services bancaires à distance. Elle intègre également des fonctionnalités liées à la gestion des cartes de paiement et des chéquiers, ainsi que des services permettant d'effectuer des opérations sur les actions cotées en Bourse, selon les fonctionnalités et conditions applicables. Pour les professionnels et les entreprises, MySalam Pro propose des fonctionnalités adaptées à leurs opérations bancaires, notamment le suivi des mouvements financiers et l'exécution de virements. Nous avons également lancé l'ouverture de compte à distance via MySalam+ . Ce service permet aux personnes éligibles d'effectuer cette démarche depuis leur smartphone, sans déplacement en agence, sous réserve du respect des conditions applicables. Il peut notamment faciliter les démarches des personnes qui résident loin de nos agences. En matière de paiements, nous proposons des cartes interbancaires et des terminaux de paiement électronique (TPE), ainsi que des solutions d'encaissement en ligne et de paiement mobile. Les fonctionnalités et les modalités d'accès dépendent des services concernés. Enfin, notre offre comprend e-Tayssir , une solution de financement permettant d'effectuer certaines démarches à distance, selon les conditions prévues. Ces différents services constituent les principaux volets de notre offre numérique. Leur développement s'inscrit dans une démarche d'adaptation progressive aux besoins des clients et aux évolutions des usages bancaires. Votre participation à ECSEL Expo s'inscrit dans la volonté d'Al Salam Bank de développer les échanges et les partenariats avec les acteurs de l'économie numérique. Quelles sont les perspectives de développement de cet écosystème en Algérie et les opportunités de collaboration entre les banques, les entreprises et les acteurs du commerce électronique ? Azouz Abdelmalek : Le développement du commerce électronique et des paiements en ligne ouvre des perspectives pour les entreprises et les acteurs bancaires en Algérie. Selon les données du GIE Monétique communiquées pour le premier semestre 2026, les transactions sur Internet ont progressé de 52 % par rapport à la même période de l'année précédente. Cette évolution illustre la progression des usages et l'intérêt croissant pour les moyens de paiement numériques. Le développement de cet écosystème repose également sur la capacité des différents acteurs à mieux articuler leurs services. Les commerçants et les entreprises ont notamment besoin de solutions adaptées à leurs encaissements, tandis que les banques peuvent contribuer à faciliter les opérations financières associées à leurs activités. Les échanges entre les banques, les plateformes de commerce électronique et les acteurs technologiques peuvent ainsi permettre d'identifier des besoins communs et d'explorer des pistes de collaboration, notamment autour des paiements, de l'encaissement et de la sécurisation des transactions. Pour Al Salam Bank Algérie, la participation à ECSEL Expo représente une occasion de rencontrer les professionnels du secteur, d'échanger sur leurs besoins et d'identifier des opportunités de collaboration adaptées à leurs activités. L'évolution de l'économie numérique nécessite une coordination entre les différents acteurs. Les échanges avec les entreprises et les professionnels permettent de mieux comprendre les attentes du marché et d'orienter le développement de solutions répondant à ces besoins. Un dernier mot ? Azouz Abdelmalek : La transformation numérique fait évoluer les attentes des clients et les pratiques du secteur bancaire. Chez Al Salam Bank Algérie, nous poursuivons le développement de nos services digitaux afin de faciliter l'accès à certaines opérations bancaires et de proposer des solutions adaptées aux besoins des particuliers, des professionnels et des entreprises. Notre participation à ECSEL Expo s'inscrit dans cette démarche d'échange avec les acteurs de l'économie numérique et de compréhension des besoins liés au développement du commerce électronique en Algérie. L’article Al Salam Bank Algérie accélère sa digitalisation est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: KP's policies will come from Islamabad now, not Kabul, says Kundi
items.description: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said on Monday that gone were the days when there would be no coordination between the Centre and the province, adding that “our policies will now come from Islamabad, not Kabul”. “Gone are the days when there was no coordination between the Centre and the province. Gone are the days when we used to fight needlessly with another province … We will have coordination with the Centre; our policies will come from Islamabad … not Kabul, Jalalabad or Kahandar. It is clear,” Kundi said at a press conference in Peshawar a day after taking the helm in KP. Kundi assumed executive control of the province after the Centre imposed governor’s rule in KP and emergency in 12 of its districts, citing security situation and alleged non-cooperation of the now non-functional provincial government. In days preceding the Centre’s move, tensions between the federal government and the PTI-led KP government had remained high, initially just over the party’s planned march to Islamabad to demand the release of its founder, Imran Khan, and later over the Centre’s accusation that its provincial government was not cooperating on counterterrorism. Federal ministers also accused the PTI’s KP government of facilitating terrorists and not taking action against them — allegations seemingly behind Kundi’s Kabul reference as Pakistan continues to raise the issue of cross-border terrorism from Afghanistan. The KP governor’s these remarks and those about about ending the lack of coordination between the province and the Centre came as he pledged enhanced support for the province’s law enforcers, who are on the frontline in the fight against terrorism. He said the new setup in the province would “not compromise on police”, pledging enhanced support and a pay raise for its law enforcers. The governor further stated that he called a meeting on security the previous day and that of the provincial apex committee earlier today. He said the Centre had “shown confidence in us” and to meet its expectations, “our first priority is the fight against terrorism”. Kundi issued a message to the army, police, Frontier Constabulary (FC) and security institutions, saying: “Our committee, this government, is standing side by side with you and will support you fully.” He said that all members of the newly-formed advisory council had today taken charge of departments assigned to them, and would share future plans. He added that during Sunday’s high-level security meeting, it had been decided that development would be the second priority of the new setup while the first would be giving whatever resources were asked for to the police and the Crime Terrorism Department. “I want to say on behalf of this government that we are by your side,” he said addressing law enforcers, adding, “Whatever weapons you want, whatever you need, we will get them to you.” Kundi stressed, “We will not compromise on our police officers and personnel. We will equip them well.” He added that yesterday, he spoke to the inspector general of police (IGP) and chief secretary, ordering that from now on, the KP police would no longer have the lowest salaries in the country. “If they are not the highest, they will at least be equal [to those of the personnel in other areas].” The governor also said that disbursements under the martyrs’ package would be increased, and the children of martyrs would be given free education. Kundi also thanked the KP public for “rejecting the circus” that had been ongoing for a few days, referring to the PTI’s long march that began on Oct 4. “I thank KP’s public that they have rejected this 13-year nuisance,” he said, referring to the PTI’s rule in the province. The governor also said that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had provided the provincial police 10 armoured personnel carriers (APCs) on behalf of the Centre. He noted that in his earlier meeting with the minister, Naqvi had assured him and the apex committee that police and security forces would be granted as much in funds as they required. “Our priority, our focus, is peace plus development,” the governor stressed. “We will work 24/7, we will deliver hope to people, to our young people, to the business community … that this is not your fight now, it is ours.” Kundi also called on young doctors who had been striking in the province, urging them to end their strike and assuring that their issues would be solved. He also addressed university staff that were protesting over salaries and employment. Additionally, he called on the business community, saying that he would work with them to solve their issues. “When there is peace here, people will come to do business and investment … and the youth will have employment,” he added. Kundi also criticised the PTI and accused it of to “fight their case” to the Centre, adding, “We will fight our case with arguments, not with abusive language.” Responding to a question, he said that work was being done on restoring internet services, and that the roads would also be opened up again in a day or two and life would return to normal. Separately, the interior minister posted about the provision of APCs on X, saying that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had directed the immediate transfer of the vehicles in view of the prevailing security situation in the province. “The fight against terrorism is our collective responsibility,” Naqvi said. “The federal government stands firmly with KP police and will extend every possible support to defeat terrorism and protect our people.” Earlier in the day, Naqvi held a meeting of the newly established Area Development Secretariat in KP. The ADS has established in KP districts placed under emergency to “restore law and order, safeguard the security of the citizens of Pakistan and ensure good governance and development”, according to an Oct 11 government order. In his meeting, Naqvi said that consulting the tribal elders was the “most important” at this point in the fight against the terrorism in KP. “We need to ask these (tribal) representatives about what their issues are so we can resolve them,” he said, reiterating the need to empower the KP police and law enforcement. “If we are spending Re1 in other parts of KP, we need to spend Rs3 here,” Naqvi said. Commenting on ADS, he emphasised that the federal government had established a separate secretariat to specifically deal with the problems of the 12 districts under emergency. “KP is a single province,” he clarified, rejecting the impression that the establishment of ADS was an attempt to dissociate the merged districts from the province. “We will work collectively in these 12 regions,” Naqvi said, adding that the PM was also overseeing the developments. Kundi, Naqvi chair apex committee meeting Earlier in the day, Kundi and Naqvi co-chaired a meeting of the provincial apex committee, a day after the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in the province. Addressing the meeting, Kundi — who is now in charge of running the province — asserted that under the new set-up, tackling terrorism would be the priority. “We can sacrifice our development, but never security,” Kundi vowed as he noted a “lack of synergy” in counterterrorism efforts in the province. “Now it will show that there is (synergy),” he said, adding that the administration will “fulfil the demands of the Counter-Terrorism Department and police”. He stressed that the administration will “work 24/7” as the federal government and the “people had put their faith in us”. “We have to show the difference,” Kundi said, adding that there was no time for holidays or weekends. He stressed that the administration was moving towards “result-oriented” actions, rather than cosmetic measures. Noting the scourge of terrorism in the province, the governor said that the “people have no freedom to live, travel and do other things” in districts such as Dera Ismail Khan, Tank and Waziristan. He called for working towards restoring freedom of movement for people in terrorism-affected districts. “People from our province also want peace, prosperity and development,” he said. Kundi expressed the hope that the new administration be remembered well. “It should be written in history that these people came and restored peace in the province,” he said. The governor added that he will hold apex committee meetings regularly. Co-chairing the meeting alongside Kundi, Naqvi remarked: “Today is the first time I can proudly say that the federal and the provincial governments are on the same page. “In the past 2.5 years, we have seen many ups and downs,” Naqvi said. The minister stated that the most difficult work was that the war against terrorism was being fought with “no backend support”. Criticising the PTI-led government, he said: “It was the [provincial] government’s job to lead the war against terrorism, but they did not do it. They kept bowing their heads only because they did not want to compromise. “But any war, no matter how many resources you have, cannot be won until the government leads it,” he stressed. “Not once, not twice; we requested them to work with us dozens of times,“ Naqvi emphasised. “One thing I will ask you to note is that this is the same force, these are the same people, but the only difference you will see is that … the same people will show you results.” He further said: “It’s not like things will change in a day; there will be difficult times. But all of us, including the governor, police, administration, and the federal government. “We have to face and defeat them together. Our intentions are pure; God will help us produce results.“ According to an official handout, the forum directed relevant institutions to ensure “coordinated, effective and decisive” steps for eradicating terrorism and establishing sustainable peace. “The forum made it clear that intelligence-based operations against terrorist activities would continue and all available resources would be utilised to improve the law and order situation,” it said, adding that the need to improve the operational capability of police and the CTD was also stressed. The body decided to provide these departments with modern equipment, necessary vehicles, effective weapons, required personnel and all other necessary resources. It was also agreed during the meeting that the resolution of problems being faced by the people, provision of basic facilities and service delivery at people’s doorstep would be ensured, the handout said. For this purpose, suggestions from the public, their needs and priorities of the local population would be considered during policymaking, it added. Kundi meets chief secretary, police chief Earlier in the day, Kundi chaired a high-level security meeting with the new chief secretary , Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam Irfan, newly appointed Home Affairs Adviser Kifayatullah Khan, and Inspector General Zulfiqar Hameed. In a post on X, Kundi said the meeting reviewed the security situation and counterterrorism efforts in KP. “Our police officers stand on the front lines of this fight, making immense sacrifices to protect our people. Their welfare, fair compensation and the future of their families must remain a priority.” He expressed his administration’s commitment to “strengthening the police and CTD and ensuring our personnel receive the support they deserve”. “Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has sacrificed enough. Our priority is to protect our people and restore lasting peace,” the governor declared. Kundi also met Minister for States and Frontier Regions Amir Muqam, who called on him at the Governor House, state-run APP reported. The two leaders exchanged views on the prevailing situation in the province, with particular focus on maintaining peace, strengthening security and addressing issues affecting the lives of the people. They emphasised the need for effective measures and close cooperation to improve the law and order situation and eliminate terrorism. Kundi and Muqam contended that the people of KP had rejected the politics of chaos and confrontation, stressing that peace, stability and public welfare should remain the top priorities. They reaffirmed their commitment to extending all possible cooperation and taking practical steps to counter security challenges and promote stability in the province. A day earlier, Kundi addressed the first meeting of the KP Advisory Council — formed by the federal government after the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule — where he outlined similar directions. “We have to fast-track things. There will be zero tolerance for corruption. Things should be done in a timely manner,” he said, adding that they would have to demonstrate a clear difference from the work done by their predecessors. Sunday’s directives came after a meeting of the federal cabinet deliberated on the security situation in PTI-led KP. During the meeting, the cabinet noted the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Subsequently, the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and governor’s rule under Article 234. Soon after, it also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in the province. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. Meanwhile, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre sought to explain that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. 61 law officers removed; 27 new appointed Following the proclamation of emergency in KP, the provincial law department de-notified 61 law officers of the advocate general’s office. These included 26 additional advocates general (AGs), 31 assistant AGs and four advocates-on-record (AORs), according to a notification issued late on Sunday and seen by Dawn . Another notification, dated Oct 11, was issued to appoint 27 new law officers, including 12 additional AGs, 13 assistant AGs and two AORs. Out of these, six additional AGs, eight assistant AGs, and one AOR were stationed in Peshawar, along with an assistant AG in the Peshawar Service Tribunal. One additional AG and one assistant AG were each stationed in DI Khan, Bannu, Swat and Abbottabad. Two additional AGs and an AOR were placed in Islamabad to represent KP. The government had already de-notified then-AG Shah Faisal Uthmankhel and replaced him with a senior lawyer, Sanaullah, who was earlier serving as an additional AG representing the federal government. Additional input by Waseem Ahmad Shah

items.title: Governor Oyebanji dissolves cabinet, retains three
items.description: By Rotimi Ojomoyela, Ekiti Ekiti State governor, Biodun Oyebanji, has dissolved the State Executive Council after holding a valedictory session with members of the cabinet. The session, held at the Exco Chamber, Governor’s Office, Ado-Ekiti, marked the final gathering of the cabinet members as the Oyebanji administration prepares for a new tenure. The session commenced with hymns, praise songs and thanksgiving to God in appreciation of His goodness and guidance throughout the administration’s first four years. Oyebanji described members of his dissolved State Executive Council as a formidable team whose contributions helped his administration deliver on its promises to the people. He expressed gratitude for the divine grace, wisdom and opportunity to serve the people of Ekiti State, noting that his administration had remained committed to making the state a better place for everyone to live. He commended the cabinet members for their support and contributions to the implementation of his administration’s programmes and policies, assuring them that he would continue to maintain contact with them. Governor Oyebanji, however, clarified that the dissolution does not affect the Secretary to the State Government, Professor Habibat Adubiaro; the Chief of Staff, Mr Oyeniyi Adebayo; and the Chief Press Secretary, Mr Olayinka Oyebode, who will remain in their respective positions. In their separate remarks, members of the dissolved State Executive Council recounted their experiences in governance and expressed appreciation to the Governor for the opportunity to serve the state under his leadership. The event also featured the cutting of a valedictory cake to mark the end of the cabinet’s tenure. Governor Oyebanji, who was re-elected in the June 20 governorship election, is scheduled to be sworn in for a second term on Friday, October 16, 2026. His re-election will see him begin another four-year tenure as Ekiti State Governor. The post Governor Oyebanji dissolves cabinet, retains three appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Achakzai draws Balochistan parallel as he flays Centre over governor's rule in KP
items.description: National Assembly Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai on Monday drew a comparison between Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, criticising the government’s move to impose emergency and governor’s rule in the former. The federal government on Sunday imposed emergency in 12 districts of KP, and placed the province under governor’s rule, taking note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif chaired the federal cabinet meeting that approved the measure, and said regarding terrorism in KP and Balochistan that “the way common citizens are being martyred, the way police officials and security officials, children and mothers [..] there can be nothing more heart-wrenching”. Speaking to media outside the Parliament House on Monday, Achakzai claimed that there was no writ of the state in half of Balochistan. “But you don’t impose it there, because the chief minister there is your favourite,” he alleged. Achakzai’s claim of a lack of the state writ in half of Balochistan was apparently in connection with the security situation in the province. Both KP and Balochistan have been facing terrorism, and according to the data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), 199 terrorist attacks were recorded in August across Pakistan, out of which KP, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks, while Balochistan recorded 89. Speaking alongside Achakzai, Senate Opposition Leader Raja Abbas Nasir also drew the Balochistan parallel. “If terrorism and peace were an issue … you should have imposed emergency in Balochistan first,” he said. Voicing his criticism of the government’s Oct 11 move, he said: “They call themselves the torchbearers of the law and the Constitution. However, they first attacked the Constitution by coming into power through Form-47 and now by signing the orders of imposing emergency against a government that held a two-thirds majority.” ‘Assault on democracy’ In his remarks assailing the Centre’s move, Achakzai said, “This will not be tolerated. It is the responsibility of everyone who values Pakistan and democracy to unite against this.” He said parties in the opposition would be asked to announce a “democratic struggle” against the move from tomorrow in areas where they had influence. “We will not abuse anyone; we will not fire bullets — we don’t have any — and we will not throw even a stone on anyone.” He said the move was an “assault on Pakistan’s Constitution and democracy”. “It is the duty of every Pakistani, whether he is a judge, general, in government or not in government, to resist this.” Centre’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP followed weeks of political tensions, with the PTI intending to march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. The march was led by suspended KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. Achakzai said Afridi was just demanding access to and medical treatment for Imran. He reiterated the demand for access to Imran and assured that the PTI leaders would not disclose the details of their conversation with Imran if meetings were allowed. They would only inform the public about his health condition, he said. He added that the opposition was still willing to hold negotiations with the government, but would also “continue its struggle against this system”. “They say that Mehmood doesn’t want to meet. Am I mad? Pakistan is not just the Prime Minister’s House or the speaker’s chamber; Pakistan is bigger than that,” added Achakzai, who has said that he would not hold any meetings with government representatives at the Prime Minister’s House or Office or at the chamber of the NA speaker. He said he was ready to hold a meeting at anyone’s personal residence. Achakzai then invited other political parties to attend a planned all-parties conference to discuss how the country should be run. Gohar to approach PHC PTI Chairperson Barrister Gohar Khan was also present on the occasion and announced that he would challenge the federal government’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP in the Peshawar High Court (PHC) tomorrow (Tuesday). Moreover, a parliamentary party meeting the same day would decide on how to stage a protest in Parliament, he added. “We will raise our voice at every forum. Our long march and protest are ongoing,” Barrister Gohar said, adding that the party would not accept emergency and governor’s rule in KP. “Whatever happened on October 11 should not have happened. October 11 will be remembered as a black day in Pakistan’s democratic history,” he said. In a statement, the PTI particularly lambasted the PML-N and its ally PPP, saying the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule would add another “black mark” to their democratic credentials. PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram, in the statement, accused both parties of supporting undemocratic and unconstitutional measures while invoking the slogans of democracy. Terming Oct 11 a “black day for democracy”, Akram asserted that neither PTI nor the people of KP would accept the “unconstitutional, undemocratic and unlawful imposition of governor rule and emergency in the province, or the removal of its elected government”. He announced that the party would continue its peaceful democratic struggle through the courts, parliament, provincial assemblies and public mobilisation until justice was achieved. Akram said that the PPP and PML-N should be judged against their political records rather than their repeated claims of championing democracy. He recalled that PPP founder and former prime minister, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, dismissed the Balochistan government led by Sardar Attaullah Mengal in 1973, followed by governor’s rule and a prolonged confrontation with provincial leadership. Akram also referred to governor’s rule in the then North-West Frontier Province during ex-PM Benazir Bhutto’s government in 1994, its imposition in Punjab under then-President Asif Ali Zardari in 2009, and the removal of the Balochistan government led by Nawab Aslam Raisani in 2013. Criticising the PML-N, Akram cited the 1997 attack on the Supreme Court by party supporters, the nationwide emergency imposed during ex-PM Nawaz Sharif’s government in 1998 , the “theft” of PTI’s electoral mandate in the February 2024 general elections , the subsequent usurpation of its reserved seats , and the passage of Constitutional amendments, adding that these actions further undermined democratic principles and the public’s electoral mandate. The PTI information secretary urged political leaders to learn from the events of 1971, recalling that the Awami League had won a majority in the 1970 general elections but was unable to assume power through a democratic transfer. He said that the failure to respect the electoral outcome and the political confrontation contributed to a national tragedy whose consequences remain deeply significant. “Pakistan cannot afford to repeat the mistakes of denying political representation or marginalising smaller provinces, as national unity depends on constitutional rule, respect for the people’s vote and meaningful provincial autonomy,” Akram stressed. He questioned the federal government’s justification for suspending the KP government, adding that terrorism required coordinated national action rather than political confrontation. Referring to figures by the Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), he said fatalities involving security personnel and civilians in KP had declined by 16 per cent during the first nine months of 2026, while nationwide fatalities had increased by 9 per cent, partly amid worsening violence in Balochistan. The PTI leader called for a transparent assessment of these figures and the effectiveness of security policies. Outlining the party’s next steps, he said that PTI would “challenge the decision before the courts, pursue all available constitutional remedies and raise the matter in parliament, provincial assemblies and other relevant forums”. He said the party would continue peaceful public mobilisation until the elected government’s authority and the constitutional rights of the people of KP were restored. The information secretary demanded the “immediate reversal of the emergency and governor’s rule, the restoration of the elected provincial government and meaningful dialogue to resolve the country’s political crisis”. KP Bar Council announces strike Separately, the KP Bar Council expressed its concern over the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule, and announced a strike of court proceedings tomorrow (Tuesday). In a statement issued on Monday, the bar claimed the move was aimed at removing the provincial government over “political differences”. It stressed that such an “extraordinary measure” must be subject to full compliance with the relevant constitutional requirements and prescribed procedures. “The use of the federal structure for any political purpose raises serious concerns regarding parliamentary democracy and provincial autonomy,” it noted, terming the move a violation of KP’s autonomy. The bar council expressed its determination that the legal community will play its role in the restoration of democracy and vowed not to remain “silent spectators”. It further said the bar will hold an emergency meeting on Oct 17 to discuss its future course of action. The statement also demanded the immediate reopening of roads so routine life could be restored.

items.title: 1 031 boules de chanvre indien interceptées, deux convoyeurs dans les filets de la police
items.description: La Police républicaine du Bénin a annoncé, ce lundi 12 octobre 2026, la saisie de 1 031 boules de chanvre indien à Bantè, dans le cadre de la lutte contre le trafic de stupéfiants. Deux ressortissants togolais, soupçonnés d’assurer le transport de cette cargaison à bord d’un minibus, ont été arrêtés au petit matin du dimanche 11 octobre. Une opération de contrôle routier a permis de mettre au jour une importante cargaison de chanvre indien sur l’axe de Bantè. Selon les informations rendues publiques par la Police républicaine, l’intervention fait suite à un renseignement transmis par le commissariat d’arrondissement de Bassila, faisant état d’un véhicule suspect transportant des munitions de calibre 12 millimètres. Alerté, le commissaire de Bantè a immédiatement ordonné une mission de contrôle. Le dispositif déployé a permis d’intercepter, après une course-poursuite, un minibus occupé par deux quadragénaires originaires de Kouloumbé, au Togo. La fouille du véhicule a réservé une autre découverte aux policiers. À la place des munitions signalées, ils ont trouvé 1 031 boules de chanvre indien réparties dans 11 sacs de jute. Pour tenter de masquer l’odeur de la marchandise, les convoyeurs présumés avaient utilisé de la sciure, des copeaux et des écorces d’arbres. Entendu par les enquêteurs, l’un des suspects aurait déclaré que le chargement avait été effectué à Aworo, dans la commune de Bassila, et devait être acheminé jusqu’à Kétou, dans le département du Plateau. Cette saisie témoigne de l’importance du renseignement et de la coordination entre les unités de la Police républicaine dans la lutte contre les trafics illicites. La cargaison a été saisie et les deux hommes devront répondre des faits qui leur sont reprochés devant le procureur de la République. L’enquête devra permettre de faire la lumière sur les conditions de transport de cette drogue et d’établir les responsabilités éventuelles dans cette affaire. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article 1 031 boules de chanvre indien interceptées, deux convoyeurs dans les filets de la police est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Saudi minister vows ‘serious response’ to Houthi attacks on airports
items.description: Saudi Arabia’s energy minister has vowed a “serious” response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom’s airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement. “The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious,” Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh. On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital’s King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure. The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for “brutal Saudi aggression” against areas they control in western Yemen. The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday. A Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen’s Red Sea coast and other areas. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government’s rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a “maritime embargo” against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing. Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen’s south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea. They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel’s war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis. Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

items.title: N267bn in education funds lie idle as 70% of Nigerian children can’t read
items.description: …states it is yet to access N65bn counterpart funding …FG, the World Bank move to tighten budget planning, spending on schools, primary healthcare …NPHCDA revitalises 3,504 PHCs, disburses N77.7bn to 8,309 facilities By Joseph Erunke, Abuja More than N267 billion in released basic education intervention funds remained unspent as of August 2026, while over N65 billion in counterpart funding was yet to be accessed by states, the federal government has disclosed, raising fresh concerns over the management of resources meant to improve learning outcomes across the country. The revelation comes amid an alarming education crisis, with about 70 per cent of Nigerian children of primary school age unable to read and understand a simple text, according to the Universal Basic Education Commission, UBEC. The figures have brought renewed attention to the disconnect between government spending commitments and the delivery of essential services, particularly as Nigeria continues to grapple with poor learning outcomes, inadequate educational infrastructure and gaps in access to quality primary healthcare. Against this backdrop, the federal government, in partnership with the World Bank and other stakeholders, has moved to strengthen state-level budget planning and execution, insisting that public resources must be tied directly to clearly defined priorities and measurable results. The intervention is being pursued under the Human Capital Opportunities for Prosperity and Equity–Governance Programme, HOPE-GOV, through a technical capacity-building workshop on Disbursement-Linked Indicator 2, DLI 2, which focuses on improving state budget planning and execution for basic education and primary healthcare. Speaking at the workshop in Abuja on Monday, the Executive Secretary of UBEC, Dr Aisha Garba, who was represented by the commission’s Coordinator for HOPE-GOV and Director of Teacher Professional Development, Maryam Sani Dangaji, said the huge sums of unutilised funds underscored the need for a fundamental shift in how states planned, budgeted and spent money allocated to basic education. She maintained that increasing allocations alone would not resolve the country’s education challenges unless governments strengthened accountability, improved expenditure efficiency and ensured that available resources translated into better learning outcomes. “Spending more will not achieve this by itself; we must spend better,” she said, stressing that every naira spent on classrooms, instructional materials and teacher training must produce tangible improvements in children’s ability to read, write and count. According to her, the challenge is not merely to provide more funding but to ensure that resources reach the schools and communities where they are most needed. Under the HOPE-GOV framework, states are expected to prepare consolidated education plans, align their budgets with those plans and ensure that approved expenditure is implemented within established performance limits. The approach is designed to strengthen the relationship between government priorities, budgetary allocations and actual service delivery, while encouraging states to deploy scarce public resources more efficiently. Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, Dr Deborah Odoh, said the quality of government spending depended largely on the strength of the systems through which public resources were planned, allocated and utilised. She said budgeting must not be treated as an isolated administrative exercise but as the financial expression of government priorities and development plans. Odoh, who declared the workshop open, said the preparation of the 2027 fiscal-year budgets offered states an opportunity to address weaknesses in their planning and expenditure processes. According to her, state development plans, sector policies, annual operational plans and consolidated workplans must be properly linked to annual budgets to ensure that allocations reflect identified needs and realistic implementation costs. For primary healthcare, she said, annual operational plans should provide the basis for identifying and prioritising expenditure, while the annual consolidated work plans for basic education should establish a clear connection between sector priorities and budget allocations. She explained that the workshop was designed as a practical exercise in which participating states would review their actual plans, workplans, budgets and resource information rather than merely receive theoretical presentations. The sessions would examine how sector priorities were costed and reflected in budgets, how expenditure was classified under the National Chart of Accounts, and how proposed activities could be reconciled with available resources and budget ceilings. Odoh emphasised that the objective was not for the Federal Government or technical experts to prepare state budgets but to strengthen the capacity of state institutions to manage their own planning and budgeting processes effectively. She urged participating states to identify existing weaknesses, agree on corrective measures and establish clear responsibilities and implementation timelines. The permanent secretary added that technical support would continue after the workshop to help states address outstanding issues and sustain the alignment of their plans and budgets. National Coordinator of the HOPE-GOV Programme, Dr Assad Hassan, said the initiative was intended to move states beyond preparing development plans to ensuring that those plans translated into funded priorities and measurable outcomes. He said the workshop represented an important step towards strengthening the institutional systems required to improve the delivery of basic education and primary healthcare. “We are here to move from plans to priorities, from priorities to budgets, and from budgets to results,” Hassan said. According to him, meaningful improvements in education and healthcare cannot be achieved simply by increasing government expenditure without addressing weaknesses in planning, budgeting, implementation and accountability. He said the workshop would help states identify gaps in their existing systems, improve the alignment of annual operational plans and consolidated workplans with their 2027 budgets, and strengthen the use of programme-based budgeting. Other areas of focus include project prioritisation, costing, mapping and geo-tagging, as well as reconciling sector plans with available fiscal resources. Hassan said the ultimate objective was to ensure that every participating state left the exercise with a clearer understanding of the reforms required and practical steps for implementing them. The Nigeria Governors’ Forum Secretariat also stressed the need for state governments to ensure that their budgetary commitments to education and primary healthcare translated into services that citizens could access. Dr Chinekwu Oreh, a senior health specialist and representative of the secretariat’s Executive Director of Programmes and Partnerships, said the success of government policies in the two sectors depended on realistic plans, credible budgets and the timely release and utilisation of approved funds. She noted that primary healthcare facilities and classrooms were where government commitments to human capital development ultimately became visible to citizens. Under DLI 2, she explained, state was expected to ensure that approved budgets for basic education and primary healthcare were based on their consolidated work plans and that expenditure remained within established budget performance limits. She said the ongoing 2027 budget preparation process provided an opportunity for states to address weaknesses identified during the programme’s Year Zero verification. Oreh added that the Nigeria Governors’ Forum would continue to support states through technical assistance and peer learning aimed at improving budget credibility, strengthening implementation and promoting timely publication of transparent fiscal information. She urged state officials to use the workshop to develop practical solutions that could be implemented immediately, rather than treat it as another routine capacity-building exercise. While education financing remains a major concern, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency, NPHCDA, outlined ongoing efforts to strengthen primary healthcare delivery through improved infrastructure, financing, workforce development and accountability. The agency’s Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer, Dr Muyi Aina, represented by the HOPE-PHC focal person, Onesirosan Omawumi Daibo, said 3,504 primary healthcare centres had been revitalised, with work continuing at another 930 facilities. The intervention forms part of the Federal Government’s target of revitalising 17,600 primary healthcare facilities over four years. Aina also disclosed that N77.7 billion had been disbursed through the Basic Health Care Provision Fund, BHCPF, to 8,309 primary healthcare facilities across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory between 2023 and the first quarter of 2026. According to him, the agency is expanding coverage towards a target of 13,521 facilities under the fund. To improve financial accountability, the agency has deployed its BHCPF Financial Management System application in 5,071 facilities across 21 states, while 774 performance and financial management officers have been deployed across local government areas to monitor performance and financial management at facility level. On workforce development, Aina said 78,054 frontline health workers had been trained towards a four-year target of 120,000. He added that the agency had incentivised the recruitment of 19,758 skilled birth attendants across 22 states and 3,876 community-based health workers across 10 states. Funding had also been secured to support the recruitment of an additional 3,629 skilled birth attendants and 11,200 community-based health workers in 26 states and the FCT, he said. Aina stressed that sustainable improvements in primary healthcare required adequate financing, costed workplans, effective implementation and accountability for results. He urged state governments to ensure that their 2027 budgets provided for functional primary healthcare facilities, adequately trained personnel, essential medicines, basic equipment and improved access to services for mothers, children and other vulnerable populations. To address weaknesses in basic education planning and financing, UBEC said it was implementing reforms intended to improve the identification of needs, allocation of resources and monitoring of expenditure. Among the measures are the revamped Basic Education Action Plan, BEAP, a digital Basic Education Action Plan Management System, BEAPMS, revised UBE Intervention Fund Guidelines and a 10-year strategic roadmap covering 2026 to 2035. The BEAP is designed to provide states with a consolidated framework for identifying and prioritising their basic education needs, while BEAPMS will support digital submission of plans, tracking of fund utilisation and publication of information on resources accessed by states from UBEC. The revised intervention fund guidelines are intended to enable states to direct resources towards areas of greatest need, rather than concentrating only on the construction of new classrooms. UBEC also called on state officials to strengthen coordination among ministries of education, finance, budget and planning, state universal basic education boards and local government education authorities. It urged states to monitor budget execution quarterly, publish relevant documents promptly and ensure that their budgets reflected approved sector plans. The commission said it was prepared to provide technical assistance through its desk officers, BEAPMS team and planning experts. The workshop brings together state officials responsible for budget and planning, primary healthcare, basic education and programme coordination, alongside representatives of the Federal Ministry of Finance, NPHCDA, UBEC, the Nigeria Governors’ Forum, the World Bank and other technical partners. The World Bank-supported HOPE-GOV programme operates alongside related interventions focused on primary healthcare and basic education, with the broader objective of strengthening public resource management and improving human capital outcomes. items.title: Seyi Makinde: Can APM presidential candidate ‘travel’ beyond South-West?
items.description: In Nigerian politics, the easiest promise to make is that performance will speak for itself. Seyi Makinde has built his political identity around precisely that proposition. Now, as the 2027 presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement, APM, he is asking a much bigger electorate to accept that what he says he has achieved in Oyo State can be scaled directly to Nigeria. Read Also: Atiku Abubakar’s long road to one more presidential fight Makinde, formally Oluseyi Abiodun Makinde, was born in Ibadan on December 25, 1967. His route to Government House was unusual for a politician. Politics tested that image early. Makinde, formally trained as an electrical engineer at the University of Lagos, graduated in 1990 and went into the oil and gas industry. He worked with Shell before moving through engineering and field-management roles and eventually establishing Makon Engineering and Technical Services in 1997. The business grew into the Makon Group. From Engineer to Political Contender That background matters because Makinde has consistently presented himself less as a professional politician than as an engineer who entered public life with a problem-solving instinct. In 2007, he contested the Oyo South senatorial seat on the ANPP platform and lost. He later sought the PDP ticket for the same senatorial district in 2011 and failed at the primary. In 2014, he pursued the PDP governorship ticket for the 2015 election, was unsuccessful, moved to the Social Democratic Party, SDP, and contested the governorship, finishing third with 54,740 votes. The Defeats Before Government House Those defeats were politically instructive. Makinde was learning that money, professional reputation and personal ambition could open the door to politics, but they could not by themselves command its machinery. He returned to the PDP in 2017, secured its 2019 governorship ticket and, on his fourth major electoral attempt, won Oyo. His victory established the businessman as an executive politician. Re-elected in 2023, Makinde has made education, health, infrastructure, security and economic development pillars of his administration. His government abolished several education levies, expanded education spending, pursued road projects, supported healthcare interventions and promoted investment and agribusiness. The administration also points to regular salary payments and welfare measures for workers and pensioners. Oyo Becomes the Makinde’s Argument The record, however, deserves scrutiny beyond government scorecards. Much of the evidence used to describe Makinde’s performance comes from the administration itself, while supporters credit him with fiscal discipline, visible infrastructure and a comparatively business-friendly environment. Critics can reasonably ask whether state-level achievements demonstrate the capacity to manage Nigeria’s vastly more complicated federal system, security architecture and fiscal pressures. Performance Meets Political Reality That question follows him into the APM. Makinde remains identified politically with the PDP, yet the party that once carried his ambitions did not become his 2027 vehicle. The APM convention in Bauchi on August 13 formally presented him as its presidential candidate, with Bauchi Governor Bala Mohammed emerging as national leader. Makinde has argued that Nigerians should judge leaders by measurable results, while calling for a stronger opposition and greater devolution of powers to states. Why APM Chose Him The choice is revealing. For APM, Makinde offers an incumbent governor with an executive record, national name recognition and a technocratic profile at a time when opposition parties are struggling to convert dissatisfaction with the ruling APC into a coherent national alternative. His appeal also lies in the possibility of bridging constituencies: a southern governor with northern political connections, a businessman comfortable with policy language, and a politician who can point to two electoral victories in Oyo. His selection of former DSS Director-General Lawal Daura as running mate reinforces that calculation. It gives the ticket a security-heavy northern component and signals that Makinde understands the limits of a technocratic message. items.title: UK PM Burnham says Iran's IRGC likely behind RAF Fairford incident
items.description: LONDON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The RAF Fairford base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran but last week, US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of the planes. U.S. officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack.

items.title: Un incendio en un AVE de Renfe interrumpe la circulación en la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Barcelona
items.description: Corte en la línea ferroviaria de alta velocidad Madrid-Barcelona en plena vuelta del puente del Pilar. Un incendio en la maquina trasera de un AVE de Renfe cuando circulaba esta tarde entre las localidades zaragozanas de Ricla y Plasencia de Jalón ha motivado la interrupción de los servicios poco después de las 16.00 horas. El problema está localizado en el tramo entre Calatayud y Zaragoza, e impacta en otros convoyes operados tanto por la citada Renfe como por Iryo y Ouigo. Los trenes que avanzaban por la línea han sido detenidos en distintas estaciones, anulándose las salidas programadas para esta tarde. En total hay 27 unidades afectadas, que estaban ya en movimiento o tenían previsión de partida a lo largo de la tarde. Renfe opera 21 de estos trenes, Iryo tiene cuatro y Ouigo, dos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Saudi Arabia Faces More Attacks as It Reels From Airport Strikes
When dialogue fails and strikes speak: Is industrial action the only language government understands?
items.description: Ghana appears to be gradually developing a troubling culture in which workers must threaten to withdraw their services before their grievances receive the attention they deserve. Negotiated agreements are reached, assurances are given, deadlines are announced, and expectations are raised. Yet, in too many instances, implementation becomes another prolonged struggle. Eventually, patience wears thin, trust deteriorates, and industrial action becomes the final instrument through which workers seek to enforce their rights. This raises a fundamental question that deserves national reflection: Has industrial action become the only language successive governments in Ghana understand? It is an uncomfortable question, but one that cannot be dismissed as mere frustration. The recurring industrial disputes across Ghana’s public sector point to deeper concerns about institutional accountability, respect for negotiated agreements, labour relations and the credibility of government commitments. The issue is not simply that workers are demanding improved remuneration or better conditions of service. Rather, it is that some workers find themselves repeatedly fighting for entitlements that have already been negotiated, agreed upon or contractually earned. This distinction is important. There is a significant difference between demanding new benefits and demanding the implementation of existing obligations. The Recurring Cycle of Industrial Actions Recent developments in Ghana’s education sector provide a compelling illustration of this problem. On 1 October 2026, the Technical University Teachers’ Association of Ghana (TUTAG) commenced an indefinite industrial action following unresolved concerns over post-retirement contractual remuneration, the implementation of the agreed Scheme of Service and the treatment of academic librarians. According to the Association, some lecturers who continued serving their institutions under post-retirement contracts had not received their contractual remuneration for as long as 27 months. TUTAG also raised concerns about administrative changes affecting the career progression of Assistant Lecturers and Assistant Research Fellows. These concerns raise serious questions about fairness, administrative responsibility and respect for contractual obligations. How does a public institution benefit from the services of an academic for more than two years without settling the remuneration reportedly due to that individual? What message does this send to younger academics who are expected to dedicate their professional lives to teaching, research and national development? Equally concerning is the situation in pre-tertiary education, where the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) and the Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG) embarked on industrial action over promotion-related arrears, allowances and outstanding conditions of service. Although these unions suspended their strike on 9 October 2026 following government engagements, their leadership indicated that negotiations would continue because the outstanding issues had not been fully resolved. These developments suggest a recurring pattern: grievances accumulate, negotiations proceed slowly, workers issue ultimatums, industrial actions follow, and government intensifies its engagement. One is therefore compelled to ask why the same urgency often appears difficult to achieve before industrial action is declared. When Negotiated Agreements Lose Their Meaning Collective bargaining is an essential component of modern industrial relations. It provides an organised framework through which employers and employees negotiate remuneration, working conditions, professional development and other employment matters. However, the effectiveness of collective bargaining depends not merely on reaching agreements but on implementing them. An agreement that remains unimplemented is of limited practical value to the worker whose livelihood depends on it. From the perspective of Social Exchange Theory, employment relationships are sustained by reciprocal obligations. Workers contribute their knowledge, time, skills and professional commitment, while employers are expected to provide agreed remuneration, fair treatment and a conducive working environment. When these expectations are repeatedly frustrated, the relationship between employer and employee becomes strained. The consequences extend beyond financial dissatisfaction. They include declining organisational commitment, weakened morale, distrust of leadership and reduced confidence in established institutional processes. This is particularly troubling in the public sector, where government is expected not only to enforce labour laws but also to demonstrate exemplary compliance with employment obligations. If government institutions cannot consistently honour their own negotiated commitments, what moral authority do they have to demand strict compliance from private employers? The Government Must Also Be Heard A balanced discussion must acknowledge that governments operate within fiscal constraints. Public expenditure must be managed against competing national priorities, including infrastructure, healthcare, education, debt obligations and other essential services. It would therefore be unrealistic to assume that every labour demand can be satisfied immediately. However, financial constraints should not become a permanent justification for delayed implementation of agreements. Where government cannot meet an obligation within an agreed period, responsible governance requires early communication, transparent explanations, realistic payment arrangements and credible implementation timelines. The difficulty arises when workers are repeatedly assured that their concerns will be addressed, only for those assurances to remain unfulfilled. The question is not whether government faces financial limitations. Every government does. The question is whether those limitations are being managed transparently, predictably and in good faith. Workers deserve more than assurances that are renewed whenever a strike threatens essential public services. Industrial Action: A Right or an Unfortunate Necessity? Industrial action remains an important instrument in labour relations. Ghana’s Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651), provides a framework for resolving industrial disputes through negotiation, mediation and arbitration, as well as regulating strikes and lockouts. Ideally, industrial action should arise only after reasonable efforts at dispute resolution have failed and applicable legal requirements have been observed. Unfortunately, when workers repeatedly experience delayed implementation of negotiated agreements, strikes may increasingly be perceived as the most effective means of securing attention. This is a dangerous development for industrial relations. A system in which workers believe that dialogue produces promises while strikes produce action risks encouraging confrontation rather than cooperation. Nevertheless, workers should not automatically be portrayed as unreasonable whenever they embark on industrial action. Their grievances must be examined on their merits, including the extent to which employers have fulfilled existing obligations. At the same time, unions must remain mindful of the wider consequences of withdrawing essential services and continue to pursue lawful, proportionate and constructive approaches to resolving disputes. Industrial harmony cannot be achieved by demanding sacrifices from workers while overlooking the responsibilities of employers. The Silent Victims: Students and National Development The consequences of industrial actions are not confined to workers and government. In the education sector, students often become the unintended victims of prolonged labour disputes. Lectures are interrupted, examinations may be postponed, academic supervision is affected, and institutional calendars become uncertain. In some circumstances, these disruptions delay graduation and the transition of students into productive employment. Parents and guardians who have invested substantial resources in their children’s education are equally affected. For Ghana’s technical universities, the implications are particularly significant. Technical universities occupy a strategic position in the country’s human capital development agenda. They are expected to produce technically competent graduates, support applied research, promote innovation and strengthen collaboration between academia and industry. These institutions contribute to the development of engineers, construction professionals, technologists, entrepreneurs and other skilled personnel required for national industrialisation. Repeated disruptions to their academic activities therefore threaten more than institutional stability. They potentially weaken the human resource development system upon which Ghana’s economic transformation depends. How can a nation consistently pursue industrialisation, technological advancement and economic competitiveness while the institutions responsible for producing its technical workforce experience recurring labour instability? The answer cannot be found in blaming lecturers for defending their employment rights or dismissing students’ frustrations. It must be found in addressing the institutional weaknesses that allow avoidable disputes to escalate. Where Is the Institutional Accountability? Ghana has established institutions responsible for managing labour relations, including the National Labour Commission, the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission and the relevant ministries and regulatory agencies. The existence of these institutions should ordinarily provide sufficient mechanisms for preventing and resolving many industrial disputes before they result in strikes. Yet recurring disagreements over negotiated conditions, remuneration and implementation timelines raise legitimate questions about the effectiveness of coordination and enforcement. Are agreements being concluded without adequate budgetary provisions? Are responsibilities clearly assigned to implementing institutions? Are delays communicated promptly to affected workers? What mechanisms exist to hold public institutions accountable when commitments are not fulfilled? These questions deserve serious consideration. There is also a need to distinguish between negotiating an agreement and possessing the administrative and financial capacity to implement it. Where implementation requires the involvement of multiple government agencies, poor coordination can create delays even after the substantive issues have been settled. Such administrative difficulties should not become the burden of workers who have already fulfilled their professional responsibilities. A credible industrial relations system must provide effective mechanisms not only for negotiating agreements but also for monitoring their implementation. From Crisis Management to Responsible Governance Ghana must move away from an approach to industrial relations that appears excessively reactive. It is neither economically sustainable nor administratively responsible for government attention to intensify principally when workers threaten industrial action. A more effective approach requires several reforms. First, negotiated agreements should be accompanied by clear and realistic implementation schedules, identifying responsible institutions, funding arrangements and deadlines. Second, government should strengthen coordination among the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Employment, Ministry of Education, the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission and other relevant agencies to minimise administrative delays. Third, mechanisms for monitoring compliance with negotiated agreements should be strengthened. The National Labour Commission must be adequately supported to discharge its statutory responsibilities effectively. Fourth, government and labour unions should institutionalise regular engagement that goes beyond crisis meetings convened when strikes become imminent. Finally, public-sector labour relations must be guided by transparency, mutual respect and accountability. Where commitments cannot be fulfilled within agreed timelines, the reasons should be communicated honestly and revised arrangements negotiated in good faith. These measures would not eliminate all industrial disputes. However, they could significantly reduce conflicts arising from avoidable delays, poor communication and unfulfilled commitments. A National Problem That Transcends Political Administrations It would be intellectually dishonest to suggest that Ghana’s industrial relations challenges began with the present administration. Successive governments have confronted disputes involving teachers, university lecturers, healthcare professionals, public-sector employees and other organised labour groups. The persistence of such disputes suggests that Ghana must examine the structural and institutional weaknesses underlying public-sector employment relations rather than viewing each strike solely through a partisan political lens. Governments change, but the institutions of the state remain. Consequently, commitments lawfully undertaken by public institutions must be treated with the seriousness necessary to sustain continuity, credibility and public confidence. Industrial relations should not become a contest in which workers are expected to demonstrate loyalty through indefinite patience while government demonstrates commitment through repeated assurances. The relationship must be founded on mutual obligations. Conclusion: Must Ghana Always Wait for a Strike? A nation cannot build strong institutions on promises that are repeatedly made but inadequately implemented. Neither can it achieve sustainable development when industrial harmony depends primarily on the ability of workers to disrupt public services. The recurring industrial actions in Ghana should therefore serve as a wake-up call to government, labour unions, public institutions and policymakers. The central issue is not simply how quickly government can persuade striking workers to resume their duties. It is how effectively government can address the underlying grievances and prevent similar disputes from recurring. For TUTAG and other labour unions, the demand for respect for negotiated agreements and earned contractual entitlements raises fundamental questions of fairness and institutional accountability. For government, the challenge is to demonstrate that dialogue can produce timely, credible and measurable outcomes without the disruption of industrial action. For the nation, the responsibility is to develop an industrial relations framework that protects workers’ rights while safeguarding education, productivity and national development. Ghana must reach a point where agreements are honoured because they are binding commitments, not because workers have withdrawn their services. Until that becomes the norm, the troubling question will persist: Is industrial action the only language government understands? And perhaps the more important question is this: What will it take for government to listen before workers are compelled to strike? About the Author Dr. Isaac Aidoo is a Senior Lecturer and Head of the Building Technology Department at Accra Technical University. His academic interests include construction management, institutional resilience, sustainability and organisational performance. The views expressed in this article are his personal views. Editorial notes before submission The article is grounded in reports from the Ghana News Agency, MyJoyOnline and Ghana’s Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651). Particularly relevant sources are the GNA report on TUTAG’s strike and MyJoyOnline’s report on the suspension of the pre-tertiary teachers’ strike . The editorial is written as a personal scholarly opinion rather than an official position of Accra Technical University or TUTAG.
