items.title: Jeffrey Nortey’s viral Kanayo O. Kanayo bar gets the legend’s attention, leads to a meet-up
items.description: A clever play on words delivered at Jeffrey Nortey’s sold-out show has earned public recognition from the very Nollywood legend who inspired it, Kanayo O. Kanayo. The moment, which combines Akan wordplay with a reference to one of Nollywood’s most recognisable screen personas, has since travelled beyond the theatre, drawing attention on social media and bringing the two entertainers together. During the third phase of this year’s edition of ‘3 Faces of Jeffrey Nortey’, the Ghanaian actor and entertainer used his popular ‘Dragon’ character to deliver a bar inspired by Kanayo O. Kanayo and the familiar phrase, “Sacrifices must be made.” The line was more than a tribute to the veteran actor. It was also Jeffrey’s response to those who had questioned whether he could pull off a successful production at the National Theatre, particularly when the event flyer featured his face without a wider ensemble of stars. Jeffrey turned the doubt into an opportunity for wordplay, declaring that people should henceforth call him Kanayo O. Kanayo before delivering the punchline, “mi ka na mayɛ oo, mi ka na mayɛ.” The line draws on the Akan expression “ka na yɛ”, which conveys the idea of talking and doing, or backing words with action. Its phonetic resemblance to Kanayo’s name gave the bar an additional layer of humour, allowing Jeffrey to honour the Nollywood star while making a statement about his own ability to deliver. The moment also reflected the broader idea behind 3 Faces of Jeffrey Nortey , which brought film, live theatre and his Dragon character together in one production. From the National Theatre to Kanayo’s Instagram The bar has since travelled beyond the audience that witnessed it live, after Kanayo O. Kanayo shared a recording of Jeffrey’s performance on Instagram. In his caption, the Nollywood veteran acknowledged the Akan interpretation of the phrase, describing it as “talk and do.” His post revitalised the wordplay, as the original tribute was acknowledged by the man whose name inspired it. The acknowledgement represents a notable moment for Jeffrey in his creative journey. A punchline crafted for a live audience in Accra has now been amplified by one of the most recognisable figures in Nigerian cinema, illustrating how social media can extend the lifespan of a live performance, allowing a moment created on stage to reach audiences far beyond the venue. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kanayo O Kanayo (@kanayo.o.kanayo) From online recognition to a personal meeting The exchange later took a more personal turn when Jeffrey shared a video of himself meeting Kanayo O. Kanayo during the veteran actor’s recent visit to Ghana. The meeting brought the online acknowledgement into the real world, creating an opportunity for the Ghanaian entertainer to connect with the Nollywood legend he had celebrated through his performance. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jeffrey Nortey (@jeffreynortey1) Kanayo O. Kanayo, whose decades-long career in Nollywood has earned him widespread recognition, is frequently associated with the memorable roles and sacrifice-themed references that have become part of his screen persona. Jeffrey’s bar drew on that familiarity while giving it a distinctly Ghanaian twist. The moment also highlights Jeffrey’s approach to comedy, which often relies on layered wordplay, cultural references and double entendres. His Dragon character has become a vehicle for this style, blending humour with observations about everyday life and popular culture. In this instance, the joke carried a message that extended beyond the laughter: talking about what one can do is one thing, but demonstrating the ability to deliver is another. What began as a creative tribute during ‘ 3 Faces of Jeffrey Nortey’ has evolved into a widely shared moment, public recognition from a Nollywood icon and a personal meeting between the two entertainers. And in keeping with the message behind the bar, Jeffrey’s performance gave audiences something more than words. It gave them a moment worth remembering and sharing. Jeffrey Nortey and Kanayo O Kanayo

items.title: Bagre Dam’s Annual Floods: Scientists seek a lasting solution as Northern Ghana’s farmers count the cost
items.description: Every year, the waters released from Burkina Faso’s Bagré Dam threaten to turn the hopes of northern Ghana’s farming communities into heartbreak. Crops nurtured for months can disappear beneath floodwater, homes can become uninhabitable, livelihoods can collapse, and families can be forced to abandon the land they call home. Now, an international team of researchers has brought science, community knowledge and nature-based solutions into the search for a lasting answer. The critical question is whether governments will turn that knowledge into action before another season of destruction begins. For farming families in northern Ghana, the rainy season should bring hope. It should mean growing crops, replenishing water sources, feeding families and preparing for a harvest that can sustain households for months. But for communities along the White Volta River, the arrival of heavy rains can also bring fear. When water levels rise at Burkina Faso’s Bagré Dam, controlled releases may become necessary to protect the dam from overtopping. Although the releases serve an important safety purpose, the additional water flowing downstream can intensify flooding in vulnerable riparian communities in Ghana. For residents whose livelihoods depend on farming, fishing, livestock and wetland resources, the consequences can be devastating. The destruction does not end when the water recedes. Families may lose their income, children may experience interrupted education, and communities can spend months or years struggling to recover. The question is no longer whether these floods pose a serious challenge. The question is how Ghana and Burkina Faso can manage their shared water resources in ways that protect lives, livelihoods and the environment in both countries. A collaborative research initiative is now examining that challenge, offering a pathway towards more informed, inclusive and sustainable solutions. A recurring disaster with a devastating history The Bagré Dam, commissioned in 1992, is a major water infrastructure project in Burkina Faso, primarily serving irrigation needs. Its controlled water releases have, since 1999, contributed to serious flooding downstream in Ghana. The effects have included deaths, displacement, destroyed farmland and damage to homes and public infrastructure. Source: Ghana News Agency. The scale of the historical damage is sobering. Research documentation associated with the “Addressing Climate Vulnerability through Nature-Based Solutions using Transdisciplinary Engagement of Wetland Communities (AV-STEC)” project records that the 1999 flooding left approximately 9,000 people homeless and was associated with 52 deaths and a cholera outbreak. In 2007, about 307,127 people were reportedly affected, with emergency response costs estimated at US$25 million. The destruction continued in subsequent years. In 2018, dam-induced flooding reportedly resulted in 17 deaths and damaged 75,607 farms, alongside thousands of houses, wells, bridges and other infrastructure. In September 2022, approximately 3,000 hectares of farmland were reported damaged, affecting an estimated 2,000 farmers. In October 2023, flooding in the Kpandai District displaced more than 2,000 residents and submerged about 43 communities, according to reports cited in the research document. These figures illustrate that this is not simply a seasonal inconvenience. It is a recurring threat to human life, rural livelihoods, local economies, food security and community stability. For a farmer, losing a field can mean losing an entire year’s investment. For a household whose savings have been spent on seeds, fertiliser, labour and other farming expenses, the destruction can leave little money to begin again. And when homes, roads, bridges and schools are affected, the damage spreads beyond agriculture to education, health, transport and access to essential services. Beyond the floodwater: a crisis of livelihoods and displacement The human cost of the Bagré Dam floods extends far beyond the immediate destruction visible during an emergency. Northern Ghana’s wetlands and riverbank communities depend on the surrounding environment for food, water, income, and other resources. When flooding damages these ecosystems or makes them inaccessible, families lose more than crops and buildings; they lose part of the foundation on which their daily lives depend. The AV-STEC research identifies several interconnected pressures affecting these communities, including unpredictable weather patterns, extreme climate events, land degradation and growing pressure on natural resources. These challenges can reinforce one another. A community already struggling with drought, limited financial resources or declining soil quality may have fewer options when flooding strikes. The effects are also unequal. The project specifically considers how gender, age, income, disability and other social circumstances influence people’s exposure to climate risks and their ability to recover. Women and children, for example, can face additional burdens when water becomes scarce or household resources disappear. Women who depend on wetland products or small-scale agricultural enterprises may see their income sources threatened, while families may have to redirect money intended for education and other essential needs towards recovery. This is why a lasting solution cannot consist solely of emergency relief after a flood. Communities also need the knowledge, infrastructure, resources and livelihood alternatives that can help them prepare for future risks. AV-STEC: bringing science and communities together The AV-STEC project seeks to address these interconnected challenges through research, cross-border cooperation and practical adaptation strategies. It brings together the Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Research (C.B.C.R.) at the University of Ghana, Naturama in Burkina Faso, York University in Canada, and START International in the United States, alongside researchers, students, community representatives and other stakeholders. The two-year initiative forms part of the Climate Adaptation and Resilience (C.L.A.R.E.) programme supported by the International Development Research Centre and the UK International Development research programme. York University described the initiative in February 2026 as a US$1.4 million project focused on climate resilience in vulnerable communities across the Volta Basin. Source: York University. AVSTEC team leaders included Emerita Professor Yaa Ntiamoa-Baidu (CBCR); Prof Christopher Gordon (University of Ghana); Prof Joseph Mensah, York University; Mr. Idrissah Zeba, Naturama, Burkina Faso; and Dr. Mary Thompson, START, USA. The research pays particular attention to northern Ghana and the communities affected by the annual Bagré Dam releases. Its purpose is not merely to document destruction, but to understand the factors that make people vulnerable and identify measures that can help them adapt and initiate some pilot intervention projects. Among its central objectives are assessing climate-related risks, understanding barriers to community adaptation, developing locally appropriate solutions, strengthening climate awareness and generating evidence that can inform public policy. The research combines household surveys, in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, ecological assessments and climate modelling. It also seeks to incorporate the experiences and knowledge of the people who live with flooding. That approach is important because a solution designed without the participation of affected communities may fail to reflect the realities of farming schedules, local land use, household finances and access to water. What solutions are researchers exploring? One of the project’s most important contributions is its emphasis on nature-based solutions and locally informed adaptation. These approaches recognise that wetlands and riparian ecosystems can help support biodiversity, water availability, food security and livelihoods when managed sustainably. The project proposes examining how improved wetland management, sustainable land use, ecosystem restoration and better understanding of local climate patterns can strengthen community resilience. It also envisages pilot livelihood interventions selected in consultation with local people. Options identified in the project include wells, boreholes, water infrastructure, support for water pumps, dry season farming with irrigation, beekeeping and the rearing of chickens and small ruminants, particularly through enterprises involving women. These are proposed projects from which the AV-STEC team will select for their pilot intervention. Obviously, the value of any such intervention will depend on careful planning, community participation, ecological suitability, reliable funding and continued monitoring. Researchers also intend to develop local climate scenarios and improve the collection and use of information that could help communities and authorities better understand flooding risks. Such information could strengthen agricultural planning, improve preparedness and support decisions about when and how to communicate impending flood threats. The goal is to move from reacting to disasters towards anticipating risks and reducing the damage before it occurs. Early warnings must reach the people who need them A warning has little value if it does not reach the farmer, family or village at risk in time. In August 2025, an AV-STEC ecological team visited affected communities to examine the effects of flooding and assess how advance information about the dam releases was communicated. Project representatives reported preliminary concerns that some residents were unaware of the planned release despite an announcement by Burkina Faso’s power utility. Source: Ghana News Agency. This raises an important public-safety question: how can cross-border warnings be converted into timely, understandable and actionable information for people living in flood-prone areas? A more effective system would require coordination between the authorities responsible for dam operations, Ghanaian water-resource agencies, disaster-management officials, district assemblies, traditional leaders and community organisations. Warnings must also be accessible to people who may not have reliable internet access or who depend on local languages and community communication networks. Radio announcements, local information centres, mobile alerts, community meetings and clearly communicated evacuation guidance could form part of a coordinated system. However, warnings alone cannot prevent every loss. They must be accompanied by safe evacuation options, suitable shelters, practical support for vulnerable households and plans to protect essential services. A shared river demands shared responsibility The White Volta does not stop at a national boundary, and the consequences of decisions affecting its waters cannot be managed effectively by one country acting alone. The AV-STEC initiative therefore places considerable importance on transboundary cooperation between Ghana and Burkina Faso, and that is why the team includes researchers from both countries Its planned activities include bringing dam-management representatives, members of the Joint Transboundary Committee and other stakeholders together to discuss research findings, policy implications and possible improvements to existing procedures. This provides an opportunity to strengthen information sharing, improve coordination and examine whether dam-release planning, local flood forecasting and community preparedness can work together more effectively. The challenge is to ensure that scientific evidence becomes part of the decisions made by institutions responsible for water management and disaster prevention. Research reports, workshops and meetings are valuable, but their ultimate public benefit depends on what happens after the discussions end. Governments must consider the evidence, establish clear responsibilities, allocate resources and communicate the measures they intend to implement. The political question: when will research become action? The Government of Ghana faces a continuing responsibility to protect citizens from avoidable harm, improve disaster preparedness and work with Burkina Faso on the management of shared water resources. President John Dramani Mahama’s administration, relevant ministries, the Water Resources Commission, the National Disaster Management Organisation, local authorities and, indeed, all of us have roles to play. The immediate questions are practical: How will research findings inform national and district-level planning? What improvements are needed in early-warning communication? How will vulnerable farmers be supported before and after floods? And what mechanisms will ensure that commitments made between the two countries translate into measurable progress? These questions should be directed to the responsible institutions, which must be given the opportunity to explain their current actions and plans for the future. The researchers, for their part, have an opportunity to present evidence that can inform those decisions. Their work could help identify the causes of vulnerability, assess future climate risks and develop interventions that are better suited to the needs of affected communities. But no research team can independently deliver a lasting solution. Effective implementation will require sustained political commitment, cross-border cooperation, community participation and the resources to turn recommendations into practical measures. A chance to break the cycle The AV-STEC project offers a potentially important bridge between scientific research and the everyday struggles of northern Ghana’s farming communities. Its long-term ambition is to improve climate resilience, strengthen local livelihoods, support inclusive adaptation and help generate evidence for better policy decisions. Whether these ambitions translate into lasting change will depend on implementation, monitoring and the willingness of relevant institutions to act on what the evidence reveals. For the farmer watching floodwater approach a field planted month earlier, the debate is not abstract. It is about whether the family will have food, whether the children can return to school, whether the household can rebuild and whether next year’s farming season will bring hope rather than fear. The communities along the White Volta deserve more than another cycle of warnings, destruction, emergency relief and recovery. They deserve effective preparedness, reliable information, meaningful cross-border cooperation and practical long-term measures that protect both people and the ecosystems on which their livelihoods depend. The research has established a direction for action. The next challenge is to turn knowledge into decisions, decisions into implementation and implementation into measurable improvements in people’s lives. The water may cross borders, but responsibility cannot stop at the riverbank. For northern Ghana’s farmers and families, the ultimate measure of success will not be the number of meetings held or reports published. It will be whether fewer, if any, homes are lost, fewer farms are destroyed, fewer families are displaced and more communities can face the next rainy season with safety, dignity and hope.

items.title: Ebonyi indigenes threaten to sue Umahi over zoning, anti-Obi remarks
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: The Association of Ebonyi Indigenes Socio-Cultural in the Diaspora (AEISCID) has threatened legal action against the Minister of Works, David Umahi, over his reported comments on political zoning and the 2027 presidential ambition of Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC). The association’s president, Ambassador Paschal Oluchukwu, said in a statement on Monday that the group had given Umahi 72 hours to withdraw the comments and apologise to Obi, Ebonyi indigenes and the wider Igbo community. AEISCID said its position followed a viral video in which Umahi reportedly discussed opposition to Obi’s presidential ambition and the zoning of political offices in Ebonyi State. In the video, Umahi was quoted as saying that some Ebonyi leaders had been criticised for declaring their intention not to support Obi in the 2027 presidential election. The association also said Umahi questioned whether Obi, while serving as governor of Anambra State, had appointed any Ebonyi indigene into his administration. On zoning, Umahi was quoted as saying that it was not the turn of the South-East to produce the president or Ebonyi South to produce the state governor. He was also quoted as saying that he intended to discuss the governorship ambition of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate in Ebonyi State, Chief Ifeanyi Chukwuma Odii, with a view to persuading him to step down in line with the zoning arrangement. AEISCID criticised the minister’s reported comments, arguing that political zoning should not be used to discourage individuals from pursuing elective offices. The association recalled the 2015 governorship succession contest in Ebonyi, when Umahi pursued his ambition despite the reported preference of the then governor, Chief Martin Elechi, for the then Minister of Health, Professor Onyebuchi Chukwu, who is from Ebonyi South. The group also urged Odii to continue his political campaign and present his policy proposals to the electorate, saying voters should determine the outcome of the 2027 governorship election. AEISCID called on President Bola Tinubu to caution members of his cabinet against making comments that could heighten political tensions. It said public officeholders should promote peace, unity and respect for differing political opinions, particularly during the build-up to the 2027 general elections. The association maintained that political disagreements should be addressed through democratic engagement rather than statements that could deepen divisions among Nigerians. The post Ebonyi indigenes threaten to sue Umahi over zoning, anti-Obi remarks appeared first on Vanguard News .

(ATOP) – Cinq cent soixante-dix (570) élèves-professeurs de la promotion 2023-2026 de l’Ecole normale supérieure (ENS) d’Atakpamé ont reçu leurs diplômes de fin de formation, le samedi 10 octobre. Le ministre Gado remettant le diplôme à une récipiendaire. Après trois années de formation dans les filières Français, Anglais, Sciences de la Vie et de la Terre (SVT), Mathématiques, Physique-Chimie et Technologie, Histoire-géographie, ces lauréats sont désormais prêts à intégrer le système éducatif en qualité d’enseignants professionnels. La formation de ces agents contribue à répondre aux besoins croissants des collèges et lycées en termes d’enseignants qualifiés. Elle s’inscrit dans la politique du gouvernement visant le renforcement du capital humain et la modernisation de l’école républicaine. La cérémonie a été marquée par la présentation des innovations pédagogiques apportées à l’ENS sur initiative du gouvernement. Il s’agit de l’ouverture de formations spécifiques ciblées en mathématiques, physiques et SVT, sur une année ainsi que des Masters professionnels d’enseignement. Ces offres visent à pallier le déficit d’enseignants dans les disciplines scientifiques et littéraires au sein des collèges et lycées scientifiques à travers le pays. Vue partielle des élèves professeurs diplômés de l’ENS Le ministre délégué chargé de l’Enseignement supérieur, Prof. Gado Tchangbedji a exhorté les nouveaux professeurs à faire preuve d’assiduité, de compétence et d’adaptabilité face aux mutations technologiques et sociétales actuelles pour accompagner efficacement les futures générations pour le développement du Togo. Le directeur général de l’ENS, Prof. Donyo Agbenoko a rappelé la responsabilité éthique et pédagogique qui incombe désormais à ces nouveaux diplômés. Il les a invités à être des modèles d’excellence, de rigueur et de dévouement au service de la nation. Prof. Donyo a témoigné sa gratitude au gouvernement, en l’occurrence au Président du Conseil, pour sa politique de la promotion de l’éducation à travers la formation des formateurs. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence du gouverneur de la région des Plateaux, le général de brigade Dadja Maganawé, des autorités politiques, administratives, militaires, traditionnelles et religieuses, ainsi que des parents et amis des récipiendaires. items.title: Arsenal lose Hincapie and Zubimendi in freak double blow
items.description: Mikel Arteta said Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi would both miss Arsenal’s Champions League match with Lille after suffering freak ankle injuries in their warm-down after Saturday’s win against Leeds. Ecuador defender Piero Hincapie, a late substitute in the 2-1 victory at the Emirates, was carried off the pitch after hurting himself in the post-match session. Arsenal boss Arteta told his pre-match press conference on Monday that Spain midfielder Zubimendi also suffered an injury in the warm-down. “We had a training session planned after the game for the players that didn’t have enough minutes to get everybody the recovery day on Sunday, and to get everybody in the right rhythm, and in two very unfortunate actions, we lost two players, and yeah, not great,” he said. “We need to assess them. Today they have further scans to see where they are, and they will have a timeframe for how long they’ll be out.” The Spaniard added: “What can you do? If I knew I had a crystal ball, I’d say, ‘Guys, go in the jacuzzi, everybody, and see you tomorrow.'” Arteta confirmed both players would miss the home game against French Ligue 1 team Lille on Tuesday, adding: “Piero’s one looks a little bit more serious, I think, but we have to wait and see.” Last season’s Champions League finalists beat Napoli in their opening match in the competition last month. Arsenal are second in the Premier League, three points behind Manchester City. The post Arsenal lose Hincapie and Zubimendi in freak double blow appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Kozah/financement de l’école publique : La FESEN mobilise les acteurs éducatifs
items.description: Kara, 12 oct. (ATOP) – La Fédération des syndicats de l’éducation nationale (FESEN) a organisé avec l’appui de l’Internationale de l’Éducation (IE), une rencontre de mobilisation des acteurs du secteur pour un financement de l’éducation publique, le samedi 10 octobre à Kara. La rencontre a été couplée de la célébration en différé de la Journée internationale des enseignants. Elle est placée sous le thème « La Force du Public au Togo : Ensemble, on fait école ! ». Elle s’inscrit dans une campagne mondiale de plaidoyer pour un financement accru de l’éducation publique, et contre la privatisation et la marchandisation de l’enseignement. Le but est de renforcer l’engagement des enseignants et des communautés éducatives en faveur d’une école publique gratuite, équitable et de qualité. Il s’agit également de partager les résultats d’une étude sur le financement de l’éducation et la privatisation au Togo, ainsi que de vulgariser les messages de la campagne. Il est aussi question de recueillir les préoccupations de la base syndicale et de rendre hommage aux enseignants pour leur contribution au développement national. Les participants ont été entretenus sur les conclusions de cette étude réalisée par la FESEN et l’IE. Selon les données, la part de l’éducation dans le budget national est passée de près de 15 % en 2014 à moins de 8 % en 2026, malgré une augmentation des dépenses publiques en valeur absolue. La proportion du Produit intérieur brut (PIB) consacrée à ce secteur, estimée entre 3 et 5 %, demeure également en deçà des références internationales de 4 à 6 %. Cette étude relève également une progression des établissements privés, particulièrement en milieu urbain, avec des conséquences sur l’égalité d’accès à l’éducation, les charges supportées par les ménages et les conditions de travail des enseignants du privé. Le secrétaire général fédéral de la FESEN, Lorie Akilè-Esso a réaffirmé l’engagement de son organisation pour la dignité et la valorisation du métier d’enseignant. Il a insisté sur le renforcement du dialogue social, l’amélioration des conditions de travail, la formation continue, l’intégration du numérique et un accompagnement particulier des enseignants exerçant dans les zones rurales difficiles d’accès. Le directeur régional de l’éducation de la Kara, Bograh Fontou a salué cette initiative qui contribue à la réflexion collective sur les défis du système éducatif. Il a souligné la nécessité de renforcer les infrastructures scolaires et de faire face aux effectifs pléthoriques, tout en réaffirmant le rôle de l’école publique dans la promotion de l’égalité des chances. Les échanges ont permis aux participants d’exprimer leurs préoccupations et de réaffirmer leur engagement à relayer les messages de la campagne auprès des communautés éducatives. ATOP/AE/DHK

items.title: Why Corporate Communications Professionals Must Be Marketing-Oriented: The strategic advantage and the professional mileage
items.description: Introduction In today’s competitive, dynamic and increasingly stakeholder-driven business environment, corporate communications can no longer be treated merely as a function of writing press releases, managing media relations, organising events or protecting an organisation’s reputation. It has evolved into a strategic management function that contributes directly to organisational growth, brand equity, stakeholder confidence, customer loyalty and long-term sustainability. To deliver these outcomes effectively, corporate communications professionals must possess a strong understanding of marketing principles and practices. Marketing and corporate communications are distinct but complementary disciplines. While marketing identifies and responds to customer needs, creates value and drives demand, corporate communications builds understanding, trust, credibility and mutually beneficial relationships between an organisation and its stakeholders. When these functions are strategically integrated, they create a powerful platform for organisational success. For corporate communications professionals, therefore, being marketing-oriented is not simply an added qualification. It is a professional advantage that expands their strategic influence, strengthens their contribution to management decisions and positions them to deliver measurable value to their organisations. 1. Aligning Communication with Organisational Objectives One of the most important benefits of being marketing-oriented is the ability to connect communication activities to an organisation’s broader strategic and commercial objectives. A communications professional who understands marketing appreciates that every communication initiative should serve a clearly defined purpose. Whether the objective is to increase awareness, strengthen brand preference, attract investment, improve customer retention, influence behaviour or enhance stakeholder confidence, communication must be designed to contribute to that objective. Marketing knowledge enables corporate communications professionals to move beyond activity-based reporting, such as the number of press releases issued, media engagements conducted or social media posts published, to outcome-based evaluation. They can assess whether communication has improved public understanding, influenced stakeholder attitudes, strengthened brand preference or contributed to organisational performance. This strategic orientation makes corporate communications a contributor to organisational results rather than merely a support function. 2. Building and Managing Strong Corporate Brands A corporate brand is one of an organisation’s most valuable intangible assets. It represents its identity, values, reputation, promise and the experience stakeholders associate with it. Marketing provides communications professionals with the tools to understand brand positioning, differentiation, brand equity, value propositions and audience perceptions. With this knowledge, they can develop communication strategies that establish a distinctive identity, communicate a compelling organisational promise and maintain consistency across every stakeholder touchpoint. A marketing-oriented communications professional understands that a brand is not defined solely by its logo, slogan or advertising campaign. It is shaped by the organisation’s conduct, the quality of its products and services, its responsiveness to stakeholders and the consistency between what it promises and what it delivers. This understanding is particularly important in managing corporate reputation. By aligning brand messages with organisational values, customer expectations and actual performance, communications professionals can build credibility, strengthen stakeholder loyalty and protect the organisation’s long-term reputation. 3. Understanding Stakeholders and Delivering Audience-Centred Communication Effective communication begins with understanding the people an organisation seeks to reach. Marketing equips corporate communications professionals with the knowledge to conduct audience segmentation, stakeholder analysis, market research and behavioural assessment. These tools help professionals identify the different needs, motivations, expectations and information preferences of customers, employees, investors, regulators, communities, policymakers and other stakeholder groups. Consequently, communication becomes more targeted, relevant and persuasive. Instead of adopting a one-size-fits-all approach, a marketing-oriented professional can tailor messages, select appropriate channels and design engagement activities that respond to the specific interests of each audience. This is especially valuable in stakeholder engagement, public education, corporate social responsibility and behaviour-change communication. Understanding the audience increases the likelihood that messages will be understood, trusted and translated into meaningful action. 4. Strengthening Stakeholder Engagement and Relationship Management Modern organisations operate within complex stakeholder ecosystems. Their success depends not only on customers but also on regulators, government institutions, employees, investors, communities, business partners, civil society organisations and the media. Marketing-oriented communications professionals recognise that these relationships must be cultivated strategically rather than managed on an ad hoc basis. Relationship marketing, in particular, provides valuable principles for building trust, sustaining engagement, encouraging loyalty and creating mutual value. By applying these principles, communications professionals can develop structured stakeholder engagement programmes, establish feedback mechanisms, anticipate stakeholder concerns and strengthen long-term institutional relationships. This approach also improves stakeholder mapping and prioritisation. It enables the communications function to identify influential stakeholders, understand their interests and develop engagement strategies that support organisational objectives. The result is stronger institutional legitimacy, greater stakeholder cooperation, improved public confidence and a more favourable environment for organisational growth. 5. Demonstrating Measurable Value and Return on Investment One of the major challenges facing corporate communications professionals is demonstrating the tangible value of their work. Marketing orientation helps address this challenge by introducing a stronger culture of measurement, accountability and performance evaluation. Marketing uses indicators such as customer acquisition, conversion rates, retention, brand awareness, customer satisfaction and return on investment. Although not every communications activity can be measured directly in financial terms, communications professionals can adapt this results-oriented approach to evaluate the effectiveness of their interventions. Relevant indicators may include changes in stakeholder awareness, media sentiment, audience engagement, campaign reach, message comprehension, public trust, stakeholder participation and behavioural outcomes. By establishing clear objectives, baselines, key performance indicators and evaluation mechanisms, communications professionals can demonstrate how their work contributes to institutional priorities. This ability strengthens their case for budgets, improves resource allocation and enables them to justify communication expenditure based on evidence rather than assumptions. 6. Enhancing Crisis Communication and Reputation Management In an era of rapid information exchange, social media scrutiny and heightened public expectations, organisations are increasingly exposed to reputational risks. A poorly managed crisis can undermine years of brand-building, weaken stakeholder confidence and affect organisational performance. A marketing-oriented communications professional understands the relationship between reputation, brand promise, stakeholder expectations and public perception. This knowledge supports more effective crisis preparedness, risk communication and reputation recovery. Marketing research and audience insights can help identify emerging concerns, while brand-positioning knowledge helps ensure that crisis responses remain consistent with the organisation’s values and commitments. Furthermore, an understanding of consumer behaviour and public sentiment enables communications professionals to anticipate how different audiences may interpret an incident and respond appropriately. When integrated with sound crisis management practices, these capabilities help organisations communicate transparently, preserve credibility and rebuild trust following a crisis. 7. Driving Innovation, Behaviour Change and Public Value Marketing is not limited to selling products and services. It also provides approaches for influencing attitudes, encouraging behavioural change and promoting ideas that deliver social and public value. This is particularly relevant to corporate communications professionals working in healthcare, public institutions, development organisations and other sectors where public understanding and participation are essential to achieving organisational mandates. Social marketing, for example, applies marketing principles to encourage behaviours that benefit individuals and society. It can be used to promote preventive healthcare, encourage screening, improve treatment adherence, support road safety and increase public participation in health and development programmes. For professionals in health communication, marketing orientation strengthens the ability to understand behavioural barriers, identify audience motivations, design targeted interventions and evaluate whether campaigns achieve their intended outcomes. Rather than merely disseminating information, communications professionals can develop interventions that make desired behaviours more accessible, acceptable and sustainable. This expands the value of communication from awareness creation to measurable social impact. 8. Improving Resource Mobilisation, Partnerships and Institutional Support Marketing knowledge is also essential for professionals responsible for corporate partnerships, stakeholder relations, sponsorships, donor engagement and resource mobilisation. Organisations must often communicate their value proposition convincingly to attract investment, secure partnerships, mobilise funding and gain institutional support. Marketing provides the tools to identify prospective partners, understand their interests, articulate mutual benefits and develop compelling engagement propositions. A communications professional with marketing expertise can therefore do more than publicise an organisation’s activities. They can help position the organisation as a credible and valuable partner, develop persuasive proposals, strengthen partnership communication and demonstrate the impact of collaborative initiatives. This is particularly important for public institutions and social-impact organisations whose success depends on public trust, stakeholder cooperation, strategic partnerships and sustainable funding. 9. Integrating Digital Communication, Data and Emerging Technologies Digital transformation has significantly changed how organisations engage their audiences. Social media, websites, email marketing, digital advertising, analytics and emerging artificial intelligence tools have created new opportunities for reaching stakeholders and evaluating communication effectiveness. Marketing orientation enables corporate communications professionals to understand the strategic application of these tools. It helps them select appropriate digital channels, develop audience-specific content, interpret engagement data and refine campaigns based on evidence. More importantly, it encourages a shift from simply maintaining a digital presence to using digital platforms to achieve defined objectives. For example, social media engagement should not be evaluated solely by likes and impressions. Depending on the campaign, success may also involve increased service enquiries, improved public understanding, registrations, participation, referrals or changes in behaviour. The ability to combine compelling storytelling with data-driven decision-making gives marketing-oriented communications professionals a significant advantage in the contemporary communications landscape. 10. Expanding Professional Competence and Leadership Opportunities Perhaps one of the greatest benefits of marketing orientation is the expansion of professional capacity and career opportunities. Corporate communications professionals increasingly operate at the intersection of brand management, public affairs, customer experience, corporate strategy, stakeholder engagement, sustainability and organisational development. Marketing knowledge equips them to contribute meaningfully across these areas. It also improves their ability to engage senior management in strategic discussions involving market positioning, organisational growth, stakeholder expectations, resource allocation and performance measurement. A professional who understands both communication and marketing is better positioned to translate organisational strategy into compelling narratives, meaningful stakeholder experiences and measurable outcomes. This combination can strengthen the professional’s suitability for senior management and executive leadership roles, including Director of Corporate Communications, Director of Corporate Affairs, Chief Communications Officer and other strategic management positions. Marketing orientation therefore broadens not only what communications professionals can do but also the level at which they can contribute to organisational decision-making. 11. Applying Marketing Orientation to My Professional Practice My professional experience across journalism, corporate affairs, stakeholder engagement and strategic communications has reinforced my understanding that communication achieves its greatest impact when it is aligned with organisational objectives and the needs of the people it serves. My experience in corporate affairs and stakeholder engagement within the energy sector, including work involving brand development, institutional relationships and corporate social responsibility, has demonstrated the importance of understanding stakeholder expectations, protecting organisational reputation and communicating institutional value. Similarly, my work in healthcare communication and public health has strengthened my appreciation of the relationship between communication, public behaviour, access to services and social outcomes. In this environment, communication must do more than inform; it must build trust, address misconceptions, influence decisions and encourage people to take actions that improve their well-being. A marketing-oriented approach provides a framework for integrating these responsibilities. It enables me to approach communication through a more strategic lens: understanding the audience, defining the value proposition, selecting appropriate channels, aligning messages with institutional objectives and evaluating the outcomes of communication interventions. It also strengthens my capacity to support organisational positioning, build strategic partnerships, improve stakeholder experiences and demonstrate the contribution of communication to institutional performance. For me, marketing orientation is therefore not a departure from corporate communications. It is an extension of the discipline that makes communication more strategic, measurable and impactful. Conclusion Corporate communications professionals must be marketing-oriented because the demands of modern organisations extend far beyond the dissemination of information and the management of media relations. Organisations need professionals who can build strong brands, understand stakeholder behaviour, strengthen relationships, manage reputational risks, influence decisions and demonstrate the value of their work. Marketing provides the strategic tools, analytical mindset and results-oriented approach required to achieve these objectives. When integrated with communication expertise, it transforms the communications function from a largely operational service into a strategic contributor to organisational performance, competitiveness and sustainability. For professionals seeking to advance their careers, marketing orientation offers significant professional mileage. It broadens their competencies, improves their contribution to management, strengthens their capacity to demonstrate measurable results and creates opportunities for leadership across corporate communications, corporate affairs, brand management and strategic management. Ultimately, the most effective corporate communications professional is not merely one who communicates well, but one who understands why communication matters, whom it must influence, what value it must create and how its impact can be measured. Marketing orientation gives corporate communications professionals the ability to connect communication with value creation, reputation with performance, and stakeholder engagement with organisational success. It is this integration that makes them more effective professionals and more valuable strategic assets to the organisations they serve.

items.title: DVLA hands 357 suspected cloned vehicles to GRA over customs duties
items.description: The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA) has impounded 357 vehicles suspected of having cloned chassis numbers or entering Ghana without the required customs procedures and handed them over to the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA). Chief Executive Officer Julius Neequaye Kotey disclosed this at the Government Accountability Series at the Jubilee House on Monday, October 12, 2026, saying the action followed the introduction of On-Board Diagnostics (OBD) devices to verify vehicle identification details and detect irregularities before registration. He explained that some individuals had allegedly brought vehicles into Ghana through unapproved routes and obtained identification details associated with vehicles on which customs duties had already been paid. This created a situation in which the same vehicle identification details could be used fraudulently, potentially allowing imported vehicles to evade the appropriate taxes and duties. “With the introduction of these OBD devices, we can detect cloned and uncustomed vehicles,” Mr Kotey said. “These vehicles are impounded and handed over to Customs to charge the appropriate taxes before they can be registered.” He said the Authority’s records showed that 357 vehicles had been impounded and transferred to the GRA as of October 9, 2026. The CEO said the intervention was intended to protect government revenue, improve the integrity of vehicle registration and prevent vehicles with questionable import or identification records from being registered without proper checks.

items.title: Kpendjal: La transformation du soja au cœur d’un atelier à Borgou
items.description: Mandouri, 12 oct. (ATOP) – Vingt transformateurs de soja, dont dix-neuf femmes, ont été formés aux techniques de transformation et de commercialisation du soja, ainsi qu’à la gestion des Activités génératrices de revenus (AGR), du 7 au 11 octobre à Borgou. Cette formation s’inscrit dans le cadre du Projet d’appui à la résilience des populations et à la cohésion intracommunautaire au niveau des territoires transfrontaliers (PARCIT), mis en œuvre par l’ONG Gestion de l’environnement et valorisation des produits agro-pastoraux et forestiers (GEVAPAF). Elle a pour objectif de favoriser l’insertion socio-économique des jeunes vulnérables. Une bénéficiaire reçoit son kit Les travaux théoriques et pratiques ont porté sur la transformation du soja en beignets, la préparation du lait, de la sauce et de la viande de soja, communément appelée « Wangash ». Les participants ont également appris les techniques de commercialisation des produits dérivés du soja, notamment les règles d’hygiène, le conditionnement, la gestion comptable et les techniques de vente. À l’issue de la formation, les bénéficiaires ont reçu du matériel et des intrants, entre autres, des bols de soja, cinq litres d’huile, une glacière, une bassine, une marmite, un foyer et du matériel de cuisine, afin de faciliter le démarrage de leurs activités. Par ailleurs, vingt jeunes ont été formés aux techniques d’embouche bovine et de commercialisation. L’adjoint au maire de la commune Kpendjal 2, Adamou Aziz a exhorté les bénéficiaires à mettre en pratique les connaissances acquises afin de développer leurs activités génératrices de revenus. Le coordonnateur du projet PARCIT, Batcha Essozimna a indiqué que ces formations répondent aux attentes des jeunes en matière d’insertion socio-économique. ATOP/BLS/JK/SED

items.title: Make Big Brother Bad for Big Business
items.description: Garrett Langley, the founder and CEO of Flock Safety, is an unlikely spokesperson for the dangers of the surveillance industry: His company says it has deployed more than 120,000 roadside cameras across 49 states. But in August, while defending his products and policies, he perhaps inadvertently showed why Americans should be alarmed by this technology. Flock caught “a ton” of “bad cops” when it rolled out a tool to identify abuse of its data, Langley acknowledged on the All-In podcast. (While Flock will soon require the tool for all of its law-enforcement clients, just a fraction of clients were using it as of mid-August. Many bad cops likely went uncaught.) He argued that Flock will force safeguards on clients, though that may lose the company business, because he wants to “sleep at night.” His competitors, meanwhile, “run more reckless”—offering video and facial recognition with their license-plate readers, for example. If you take him at his word—and I’d argue that he overstates the strength of Flock’s safeguards––it’s clear that the way the industry works is worrying even one of its biggest boosters. My own sleep has been troubled by the private surveillance industry for more than a decade. In 2014, three years before Flock was founded, I warned in The Atlantic that mass surveillance of all car trips was nearly upon us . I noted that private companies were deploying automatic license-plate readers, or ALPRs, at scale on America’s public roads, threatening a privacy we’ve always enjoyed, and that Congress should regulate the fast-growing surveillance industry. Today, if you drive in much of the continental United States, Flock may profit by selling others the means to reconstruct your movements. Opposition to this form of surveillance is now a plurality position, according to an August YouGov survey , which found that more Americans oppose the technology’s use in their neighborhood than support it. Politicians in both major parties are criticizing ALPRs, whose name has become something of a misnomer: The cameras can capture detailed images of passing vehicles, not just of the license plate. And anti-Flock activists who track clients of the company list scores of past and potential clients that have canceled their contracts or deactivated cameras in recent months. “I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology,” Jay Stanley, an ACLU senior policy analyst, told The Guardian . “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’—keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.” Still, most of Flock’s network and its competitors’ cameras remain in place. And fans of the technology want to keep it that way; they argue that there is no reasonable expectation of privacy on roads, and that a network of cameras that logs every passing vehicle is a vital tool for catching criminals. Most surveillance boosters don’t deny that serious abuses have happened or wholly dismiss privacy concerns. Instead, they urge the use of safeguards and the passage of regulations to address them. But this technology is already ubiquitous. States and localities should not permit its dangers to persist in the hope that one day, our often passive legislators will act. Instead, Americans should work to ban mass surveillance of public roads in every jurisdiction where they can secure support from elected officials until strong protections are in place. The pro-surveillance coalition has significant political influence, and some of its members employ accomplished lobbyists. The only way that it will hasten privacy safeguards is if doing so is the only way to sustain the surveillance business. Before sketching out what specific legislative protections could look like, it’s helpful to notice that popular debates about ALPRs overstate their likely benefits and understate their dangers. The primary benefit––they help catch some criminals––will grow less effective over time as knowledge of the technology and how to evade it spreads. For example, license plates are already being cloned . And as the benefits decline, the cost that law-abiding citizens pay in lost privacy will persist. It may even increase. After all, the business model–– pay us and we’ll help you catch criminals ––creates a powerful incentive for surveillance companies to address falling effectiveness with new privacy intrusions. Flock may eschew facial recognition today, but no federal law prevents it from changing its mind tomorrow, or requires that it alert the public before introducing a new tool. While evidence remains limited that ALPRs reduce crime in general or violent crime in particular, there is solid evidence that they reduce car theft: A working paper , published in August by the criminologists Scott M. Mourtgos and Ian T. Adams, found that ALPR networks are associated with an 11 percent decline in such thefts and an increase in arrest clearance (though they cautioned that clearances were already rising in the weeks before camera deployment). But if vehicle owners installed their own trackers, benefits could be had for all who opt in without imposing costs on everyone’s privacy. Some dangers of roadside cameras are well understood. The Institute for Justice maintains a database of known and alleged police abuses of the technology , including stalking and wrongful stops. And although Flock’s rollout of Audit Assistance, the tool that helps catch abuse by cops, redounds to the company’s credit, it is no cure-all: It “detects abnormal activity and flags it for Administrator review,” a Flock spokesperson clarified to me by email, which “refers to review by an authorized administrator at the customer agency—not a Flock administrator.” This leaves open the possibility that abuse will remain undisciplined by some police departments. A less widely understood danger is what might be called the foreign-adversary problem. China, Russia, and others have real incentives for gaining access to data collected by license-plate readers. Doing so could assist hostile actors in recruiting assets, blackmail, intimidation, and more. Breaching Flock would be the biggest prize––and the public is in no position to evaluate how competently the company or its competitors secure their data. If Edward Snowden could make off with the NSA’s most sensitive secrets, a systems administrator at Flock or a competitor could theoretically attempt a large-scale theft. The company (let alone the public) may not even know about it. That worst-case scenario aside, a hostile foreign actor could do damage to U.S. interests merely via the access that normal Flock clients enjoy. Thousands of law-enforcement agencies use Flock. That means thousands of targets for incidents such as a phishing attack, well-placed bribe, or blackmailing a corrupt county sheriff. What specific legal safeguards would justify the use of this technology? Figuring that out requires distinguishing between two different ways road cameras might operate. Say that a 1961 Ferrari 250 GT California Spyder is reported stolen by its owner when he arrives home from work to find the car missing from his garage, and the Highland Park, Illinois, police department puts its license plate, NRVOUS, on a “hot list” of missing vehicles. In one approach, Chicago-area license-plate readers could (if the local regulatory scheme allowed it) scan all passing cars for “hot” plates, and instantly delete data on all vehicles that are not a match. Alternatively––and this is the status quo––license-plate readers could store data from all scans, enabling people with access to the data to retrospectively reconstruct the movements of many thousands of innocents who have no connection whatsoever to any crime. (In this case, neither approach would result in the return of the vehicle in usable condition.) Defenders of the way that Flock and other mass-surveillance technologies currently function favor constantly collecting and storing data on the movements of millions of people to ensure that a tiny cohort of criminals is surveilled. But that “collect and store it all” approach is not necessary for us to benefit from ALPRs. In Germany, multiple states deploy roadside cameras. Some German states use protocols that flag “hot” license plates while deleting all scans of plates that aren’t hits. That approach offers benefits without creating a spy apparatus that captures and stores data on nearly everyone. If a collect-and-store-it-all approach endures, equally comprehensive safeguards are justified. First, companies should be permitted to retain data for no longer than a week, on encrypted, local servers; retaining data longer than permitted should be a crime. Authorization by a city council or county board of supervisors should precede installing cameras in any jurisdiction and constrain how that data are shared. And periodic reauthorization votes should be required. Second, the federal government and all of its agencies should be banned from deploying ALRP technology on public roads or from accessing data collected there. Third, state and local police should be required by statute to get a warrant to query ALPR data, whether or not federal courts consider these queries Fourth Amendment searches. Fourth, permissible reasons to query the data should be limited––for example, to investigating felonies or missing or endangered persons, or responding to imminent threats of serious injury or death. And all queries should be made by a named person whose actions can be audited. Fifth, every camera should be registered with the DMV in the state where it is located, display a physical license number on the device itself, and appear on a publicly accessible map that shows the location of all devices that capture data on public roads. Sixth, individuals should have a right to know that their license plate was queried, by whom, and for what reason; to obtain records stored on their plate; and to compel deletion and payment of damages if the record was collected unlawfully or retained beyond statutory limits. Seventh, as Mike Fox of the libertarian Cato Institute suggests , Congress should pass a law that authorizes victims of automated-surveillance errors to sue technology vendors for damages. Until Congress acts, states and localities should impose restrictions or bans, as Knox County, Tennessee , and Oconee County, South Carolina, have done . (Scores of cities have already canceled or declined to renew contracts with Flock.) In a City Journal article that argues against banning automated license-plate readers, the Manhattan Institute scholar Rafael Mangual writes , “Banning technologies in anticipation of harms that have yet to materialize is the wrong approach to policymaking. Where a technology presents genuine risks, policymakers can act to mitigate them.” But surely some potential harms, such as foreign adversaries accessing information that harms national security, or authoritarian officials exploiting networked ALPRs to threaten democracy, should be anticipated and averted rather than addressed after the fact. What’s more, significant harms related to ALPRs have already materialized. Mass tracking by the federal government is reality rather than speculation: Last year, the Associated Press reported that “the U.S. Border Patrol is monitoring millions of American drivers nationwide in a secretive program to identify and detain people whose travel patterns it deems suspicious,” and that “suddenly, drivers find themselves pulled over” and are “aggressively questioned and searched, with no inkling that the roads they drove put them on law enforcement’s radar.” And a 2015 investigation by the Electronic Frontier Foundation found that “100 ALPR cameras in Louisiana, California and Florida were connected unsecured to the internet, many with publicly accessible websites that anyone could use to manipulate the controls of the cameras or siphon off data.” Details from a few entries in the Institute for Justice database of alleged police abuses help to convey their gravity: A Georgia police chief allegedly tracked an ex-girlfriend and her teenage daughter about 600 times. In Texas, a deputy reportedly used data from tens of thousands of Flock cameras to find a woman accused by her partner of having an abortion (the deputy later claimed that he made the search out of concern for the woman’s welfare). In Lenexa, Kansas, police reportedly tracked “a writer who wrote a column critical of them,” whom they also suspected of hanging anti-police posters on city property (which the writer has denied). In Toledo, Ohio, an innocent driver was attacked by a police dog, held at gunpoint, and jailed for hours after a Flock camera misread a digit on his license plate (the Toledo police said that they took “appropriate administrative action” after the incident, which included a “verbal reprimand” for the officer involved). Getting a new privacy law through Congress is hard. Preventing its passage or watering down its provisions is easy. As a result, the intrusions on privacy just keep growing. But if people who favor and even profit from mass surveillance confronted state and local bans until adequate federal protections were in place, they would suddenly have a powerful reason to push for the speedy passage of new privacy rules. That change in incentives may be the best hope for Americans who see how quickly technology is changing and want to stand athwart the surveillance state, yelling Stop .

items.title: Appeals will not end strike, FWSC must negotiate – GAUA General Secretary
items.description: The General Secretary of the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA), Charles Jojo Aidoo, has insisted that appeals from the Education Minister will not resolve the ongoing strike by university administrators. He says the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission must engage the union and conclude negotiations on its conditions of service to bring the industrial action to an end. “We expect Fair Wages to call us and conclude whatever negotiation they want to do with us,” he said ahead of a meeting with the Education Ministry on Monday, October 12. He explained that the union expects the meeting with the Minister to focus on efforts to persuade its members to return to work, rather than direct negotiations on their outstanding demands. “Our expectation from him is to maybe appeal to us to go back to the office, and we’ve consistently told him that we respect him so much, but respect doesn’t put food on our table,” he added. GAUA declared a strike over the government’s failure to pay negotiated and approved allowances after unsuccessful negotiations. The industrial action, which is approaching its second month, has disrupted administrative services at public universities as the association pushes for action on outstanding payments and disparities in allowances and other conditions of service. The meeting with the Education Ministry is expected to explore ways of resolving the dispute, which has disrupted administrative services at public universities.

items.title: Haruna Iddrisu hails Ghana’s academic calendar as best in a decade
items.description: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu has called for the protection of Ghana’s improved academic calendar, saying the country has not enjoyed such a well-aligned schedule in the past decade. He said the current calendar, which is designed to synchronise academic activities across all levels of education and align them with universities, must be maintained to ensure predictability and a smooth transition for students. Mr Iddrisu made the remarks on October 12 during a visit to Osu Presby Boys’ Primary School to assess the situation following the suspension of a two-week teachers’ strike. He urged stakeholders in the education sector to work together to preserve the gains made in restoring stability to the academic calendar. “In the last five to 10 years, we have never had a good academic calendar like we have now,” he said, stressing the importance of ensuring that the calendar remains on track. According to the minister, the alignment of the academic calendar, particularly between pre-tertiary institutions and universities, would help reduce delays and provide greater certainty for students progressing through the education system. He stressed the need to ensure that students completing Senior High School (SHS) progress to the next stage of their education without unnecessary delays, adding that they should be enrolled in the next level once their results are released. Mr Iddrisu said a predictable academic calendar was essential to ensuring lessons were completed on time, examinations held as scheduled, and students progressed to the next level of education without unnecessary delays.

items.title: Tennis: Alexander Zverev assuré de terminer n1 mondial à la fin de l'année
items.description: Alexander Zverev est assuré de finir l'année numéro un mondial du tennis à la suite de la défaite de Carlos Alcaraz lundi au troisième tour du Masters 1000 de Shanghai, a annoncé l'ATP. L'Allemand était déjà sûr de monter à la première place car l'actuel N.1 Jannik Sinner, forfait jusqu'à la fin de la saison à cause d'une blessure au genou, va perdre ses points obtenus la saison dernière à la même époque. On sait désormais qu'il le sera aussi à la fin de la saison après le Masters de Turin car Alcaraz, 3e, a désormais trop de retard pour le dépasser après sa défaite à Shanghai contre le Belge Zizou Bergs. Zverev, 29 ans, deviendra officiellement N.1 mondial pour la première fois de sa carrière le 2 novembre après le tournoi de Vienne après avoir remporté cette année ses deux premiers titres en Grand Chelem, à Roland-Garros et à l'US Open. « C'est une saison fantastique pour moi, avec des victoires à Paris et à New York, et savoir que je vais terminer l'année au sommet du classement est un véritable rêve qui devient réalité », a déclaré Zverev sur le site de l'ATP. Le futur N.1 mondial est toujours en lice à Shanghai où il affrontera le Kazakh Alexander Bublik en huitièmes de finale. Sinner avait réussi une fin de saison 2025 exceptionnelle en remportant l'ATP 500 de Vienne, le Masters 1000 de Paris et le Masters de Turin (pour l'anecdote il avait battu Zverev lors de ces trois tournois) et son forfait va lui faire perdre plus du quart de son total de points actuels. The post Tennis: Alexander Zverev assuré de terminer n1 mondial à la fin de l'année appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Silent Football: A team, a dream, a $24,000 debt – the struggles of Ghana’s deaf footballers
items.description: Football is a game of communication. Players shout for the ball, call out instructions, warn teammates of approaching danger and celebrate goals together. Communication is constant, often happening in seconds, as players work to outthink their opponents and find a way to win. For Ghana’s deaf footballers, however, the game takes a different form. A hand signal can call for a pass. A glance can change the direction of an attack. Players must read movements, remain alert to their surroundings and rely on their awareness and understanding of one another to keep the game flowing. “Our communication depends on our eyes,” Richard Ofori, a forward said in a JoySports documentary by Haruna Mubarak titled “Silent Football: When Passion speaks without words. “As I am playing, I look left, right and behind me. I look far ahead of me. Sometimes I even call on my friends to move a bit further so that I can pass the ball to them, depending on what is happening on the pitch.” These are the men behind the Black Wonders, Ghana’s deaf football team, whose story is about more than the challenges of playing the game. It is also about achievement, national pride, financial hardship and a dream that refuses to die. Success without sufficient support Over the years, the Black Wonders have built a record of achievement, winning silver at the African level and gold in West Africa. Their successes demonstrate that Ghana’s deaf footballers can compete and win on different stages. They have represented the country with distinction, showing the ability and determination required to pursue their ambitions in the sport. For the Black Wonders, that question became particularly painful during the 2023 Deaf World Cup in Malaysia. The tournament offered an opportunity to compete internationally and carry Ghana’s hopes onto the world stage. Instead, the campaign descended into chaos, leaving players and officials far from home and pleading for help. Ghana exited the competition early, but the consequences of the trip did not end with the final whistle. A debt of $24,000 relating to hotel accommodation remains unresolved. Three years after the tournament, the outstanding amount continues to hang over the team as it looks towards another international challenge. Another dream on the horizon The disappointment of Malaysia has not ended the Black Wonders’ ambitions. Australia is scheduled to host the Deaf World Football Championships in 2027. Before the team can reach that stage, however, it must navigate qualification matches in Ethiopia later this year. The road to Australia begins with the challenge of securing a place at the tournament while preparing for another demanding international campaign. President of the Ghana Deaf Football Federation, Christopher Ekpo believes the team has the ability to make an impression if it receives the necessary backing. “I have confidence that in the whole of Africa, we are second. At the world level, we are number 14. But we are confident that when we get all the needed support, we’ll be able to do well.” Patroness for the Deaf Football Federation, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for support from government ahead of the qualifiers. “With no disrespect to Black Stars, I think if a fraction of what was given to the Black Stars was actually channeled towards the Ghana Deaf football team, we’d be amazed by what they would do for Ghana,” she said in the documentary. Minister of Environment, Science and Technology of Ghana Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings with the deaf football team For Ghana’s deaf footballers, Australia 2027 represents another chance to show what they can achieve. The dream remains alive, but the question is whether the support will come in time. The Black Wonders have already shown that they can win on the pitch. Now they need the backing to ensure that financial difficulties do not stand between them and another opportunity to represent Ghana.

items.title: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu demands merit-based admissions, appointments at Defence University
items.description: The Minister for Education, Haruna Iddrisu, has charged the governing council of the National Defence University of Ghana to make meritocracy and non-discrimination the basis for student admissions, graduation and staff appointments. He said the institution must uphold the values of fairness, professionalism and discipline associated with the Ghana Armed Forces as it develops into a specialised centre for defence and security education. Addressing the inauguration of the university’s governing council, Mr Iddrisu said there should be no discrimination based on a person’s background, beliefs or personal circumstances. “The culture of merit and meritocracy, which has always guided the Ghana Armed Forces, must be the hallmark of what defines who gets enrolled as a student, who gets registered as a student, and who gets graduated as a student and who gets appointed as an academic staff or other member,” he said. He added that there should be no basis for discrimination on the grounds of race, origin, political opinion, gender, occupation, religion, creed or disability. The minister said the council must ensure that the university becomes a truly national institution that operates according to the highest standards. The National Defence University is being established under the National Defence University Act, 2026, to provide specialised higher education for the Ghana Armed Forces and the wider security sector. Its responsibilities will include advanced strategic studies, research, policy development and the award of specialised degrees in defence and security. The governing council is expected to oversee the transition of existing military training colleges and institutions into the new university’s structure. Mr Iddrisu also announced plans to support the development of the university’s faculty, including a proposed arrangement under the 2027 GETFund formula to sponsor at least 10 faculty members to pursue studies up to PhD or professorial level. He said the institution must preserve the discipline associated with the military while ensuring that access to education and professional opportunities is guided by merit. The government expects the university to contribute to national development by improving strategic leadership and strengthening relations between the military and civilian institutions.

items.title: Oyo police arrest man who travelled from Anambra to avenge brother’s death
items.description: The Oyo State police command has arrested a man who allegedly travelled from Anambra State to avenge his brother’s death, recovering a pistol and a cartridge from him. The suspect was intercepted by operatives of the Safer Highway Patrol during a stop and search operation along Ife Road while travelling in a commercial bus, the command’s Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Ayanlade Olushola Olayinka, said. According to Olayinka, the suspect’s responses during questioning indicated that he had travelled to Oyo State to carry out a revenge killing over his brother’s death. He said the suspect was arrested following the discovery of the firearm and ammunition during the search. In a video of the suspect being questioned, he said he was working in Benue State when he received information that his brother had died at a school in Oka, allegedly after being killed by someone. “I was working in Benue State. My brother was in school in Oka. I had information that he just died in the school. That somebody killed him in the school,” he said. The suspect said he returned after receiving the news but lost his mother a few weeks after his brother’s death. “A few weeks after my brother died, my mother also died,” he added. He explained that he later received information that the person he believed was responsible for his brother’s death was living in Oyo State, prompting him to set out to find him. “Last month, I had information that the boy is living in a state, Yoruba State. I said I will find out that place where he is living,” the suspect said. During the questioning, he confirmed that he was heading to Oyo State when police arrested him. Asked where he obtained the firearm, the suspect said he bought it from a friend for ₦20,000. “I bought it from my friend. I don’t know, maybe he’s a hunter.” The suspect also admitted to belonging to the Vikings’ confraternity when asked whether he was a member of a cult group. “Yes, the Vikings,” he answered. However, when asked whether his deceased brother also belonged to a cult group, the suspect said he could not confirm it because he was not with him at school. “Maybe he belongs, maybe he does not belong because I was not there with him. I was not in the same school with him,” he said. Olayinka said the suspect was undergoing investigation to establish his connections and determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. He credited the officers involved in the operation for intercepting the suspect, adding that investigations were continuing to establish the full details of the alleged revenge plot. The post Oyo police arrest man who travelled from Anambra to avenge brother’s death appeared first on Vanguard News .
